And I think not that this rule should not be implemented, but that if we're going to keep alluding to this kind of vague notion of the image and public perception of powerlifting, we should strictly define what we feel that is. What actions do we feel are going to detract from that? Does it go as far as a lifter screaming and jumping up into the air and saying, let's go and being really happy and outwardly celebrating? Are those kinds of things going to count? I'm going to say probably not. I don't necessarily think that this rule is, and again, I'm going to try to be generous here. I don't necessarily think this rule is no fun allowed, no outward expression of joy. We're cutting all of that. But I think it does leave a lot up to interpretation. And I don't know, people are people and there's going to be people who try to take advantage of a rule if it's not clearly defined. What I mean by that is you're going to have somebody in a chair who sees a celebration from a lifter who just beat their home nation or whatever, beat their lifter that they coach and there's going to be some sort of conflict of interest. They're going to be able to interpret the rule in a way that maybe favors them and offer a war. You see where I'm going here? Sure, is that a far fetched thing to happen? Maybe, maybe not. But I think if we're going to implement these rules and consistently refer to this idea of image and values and stuff like that, we need to more clearly define them and they need to be able to be quickly referenced in all of these rules, right? See section whatever for these values that we keep kind of alluding to, right? And rule change number 19. This one is kind of just reiterating what already happens with a lot of the jury processes. This is saying that the juries may utilize an instant replay function and essentially that they're privy to, you know, camera angles and things like that to help make their decisions in potentially overturning the referees' calls on the platform. I think that there are again pros and cons to a lot of this. I think generally speaking, it's a good thing to have the jury have access to instant replays and utilize the technology that we have, right? If you watch an international championship, there is a camera angle dedicated to essentially that bench butt cam, right? There's a really bright light on the other side of it. And the camera's pointed in such a way that if the lifter's butt comes up at all, you can see that light. And I think especially with all these new bench rules and bench depth and are they using their upper body to bench too much? You know, all these kinds of things that now referees have to watch that in some cases, there have been examples where referees on the platform don't catch a butt coming up off the bench and the jury does. And I think in that case, good work. However, I also think that there has been since this kind of additional power has been given to the jury, I think there has been a real shift in how the audience, how the lifter's experience calls at the highest level. Because it does seem like it doesn't really matter what the referees say on the platform, what you're waiting for to know whether or not you've made a lift or the lifter you're watching has made a lift is whether or not the jury intervenes. And I think there have been a number of instances where the amount the jury has intervened has been more than it needed to be, more than it should have been. Not to say that sometimes they weren't the right calls. Absolutely, I think the jury exists for a reason. But I also think that the jury's function should be to intervene when calls are egregious, when mistakes have been made or things haven't been caught and they're there as kind of a fail safe. However, I feel like the way the jury has evolved in the past couple of years has been to essentially, I don't know, give a passing or failing grade to the referees in real time. And I don't think, again, if we wanna be very concerned about the image and the optics and the professionalism of the sport, I don't think that consistently undermining your IPF level referees at a world championships is the best way to do that. So, while I think, you know, I've gone off the rails here on my feelings about the jury in general, but this rule simply states that they're able to use the technology available. Beyond that, there are a few more rules that have changed, a few more things in red text. If you're reading along, but unless you're a national or above level referee, in which case, you're reading this anyways, these things probably are not going to affect you. So, I'm not gonna bother covering them and we're gonna wrap this thing up. Now, my final summary on all of this is, number one, the IPF can and should do a better job communicating with their membership when it comes to large scale changes such as this one. I believe that the IPF owes it to their membership to communicate clearly and probably in advance of these rules being implemented. The chosen method of communication being a personal post on an IPF committee members Instagram page is not an acceptable method for communicating with the membership at large. Number two, I think that we need to have a serious look at the rule book potentially as a whole from a technical linguistics standpoint. We need to use better technical language to describe the body, to describe movement, to describe position. We need to clarify these things and we need to be semantic down to the smallest level because one of the reasons I fell in love with powerlifting was its lack of subjectivity. I came to a point where it was a choice between, you know, maybe bodybuilding and powerlifting and powerlifting was number go up, I lift more than this other person, I do better, I score more, nice, right? And I think that is some of the beauty of powerlifting. And that is unfortunately lost on some level, not necessarily on a huge level, but on some level due to the wording of things in the rule book. And I think especially if we're gonna implement new rules and additional rules and attempt to make clarifications on rules that we should be really fine tuning the language we're using to do so. And number three, I think if you're still watching this, thank you, I've said a lot. === FILE: 3 Quick Bench Press Tips That Actually Work #powerlifting [PUt-P5sSjuI].en.txt ===

And finally, if you just want some quick, easy bench tips, we got a couple here. Firstly, use your back. The muscles of your upper back should be actively locking your shoulder blades into place to increase the stability of you while you bench press. Also, use your legs. Your legs should be driving into the floor, pushing you up the bench to again help improve and increase stability. Lastly, not specifically a technique thing, but more just how you should be executing. Pause your benches at least some of the time. Pausing on your chest is going to make you a stronger bench presser. It's going to make you stronger off the chest, which is where most people are weakest. And it'll give you substantial advantage in pushing your bench forwards because of that strength in the weak spot.

=== FILE: 3 Signs You Should Add Weight to the Bar [yPdo3DRgBXk].en.txt ===

Okay. So, the first indicator that you can probably go up is going to be bar speed. The bar is flying and you're moving smooth, lifts are clean, it's a good sign. If your lift feels average, maybe repeat it the next week and try to get that bar speed up before adding weight. Indicator number two, if the RP is lower than what's programmed. If you're supposed to do a set at RP8, but you rate it a six, obviously you've got room to go up. Now, to give a little bit more specifics about that, if you're one or more RPS under what's prescribed, I'd say go ahead and go up in that session. But if you're only a half RP under, count it as an undershoot. You crushed it and add weight the next week. The third indicator I've got for you is minimal technique breakdown. Yes, we need to strain. We need to push against heavy weights. And sometimes reps get a little sloppy. I don't want anybody to be terrified of tiny little nuances and changes in technique because that is normal and it is fine. But I like to apply the rule of 80% that I got from Mike Tashir. You want 80% of your reps to look about 80% good as far as technique. 80% perfect or better. Do they have only one or two minor errors to their technique on a on a hard set. You don't panic over it. You don't reduce the weights or or anything like that. I've seen lifters who hold themselves back on progress because the technique is not absolutely perfect. But this is a long-term thing. Eventually, you get to where you can correct this. If you're checking those boxes, then you're in the clear.

=== FILE: 3 Times You Should NOT Add Weight [pQXzZsI29Tc].en.txt ===

All right. So, now let's talk about three examples of when you should not add weight to the bar. I call these the three nigh nighs. I have trouble saying no. I say nigh nigh. It's easier for me. Number one, if there's too much technique breakdown nigh neigh. Now, I mentioned the rule 80%. that still stands here. But if every single rep is reinforcing breakdowns in your technique that maybe you're trying to fix, well, you're not going to be able to fix those if you're just doing bad reps over and over again. Nigh nigh. There are some edge cases where you can progress in weight and get stronger while fixing technique issues, but you have to be executing your reps well in order to do that. Number two, if you're absolutely grinding out every rep, [\h__\h] Yes, in order to get stronger, we need to strain against weight. I get it. But we also need to be able to accumulate a decent amount of volume. Training your competition lifts does not need to be a grind fest. And if you're hitting RP 111 on the second rep of what should be a set of eight, give your head a shake. Neigh neigh. The last one is if your externals are poor, right? If you're not sleeping well, if you're not eating well, if you're overly stressed, if you're feeling super fatigued, those might not be good times to be expecting to take big jumps in weight and make a ton of progression. Yes, there are times where we'll be able to progress despite externals being bad, but you should adjust your expectations and be realistic going in if you know the odds are stacked against Yeah. Yeah.

=== FILE: 5 Mistakes That Are Keeping You WEAK [5D7FqY92olc].en.txt ===

All right. So, you've been lifting for a while, but you're feeling stuck. Your squat is stuck. Your bench is not budging, and your deadlift feels glued to the floor. It's probably not because you've hit your genetic ceiling. It's likely because you're messing up at least one of these five things. Let's get into what those mistakes are and how to stop messing them up. Thing number one is nutrition. If you take your training seriously at all, well, you better have at least a cursory idea of how to eat. Your first priority should be adequate protein intake. Whether you're bulking or cutting or maintaining or gaintaining or whatever the hell you're doing, you need to hit your protein requirements. This means 1.4 to 2 g of protein per kilogram of body weight. And next, you need to have an idea about your calories. It's probably best you have some sort of plan, whether it's to bulk or to cut. Start tracking your calories. You can use something like macroactor and you can use code crab shark to get two weeks of it for free. Start tracking your body weight as well. Side note, if you want your strength to go up, being in a slight caloric surplus and gaining some weight is a great way to do it. Thing number two is sleep. It's really important for everybody out there to make sure that you're practicing safe sleep. Try and get at least 7 hours every night. Adjust the temperature in your room to be cooler if you can. Always rise and go to sleep at the same time. Get off your devices an hour or so before you go to bed. and try to stay off of it for an hour or so after you wake up. If you want to log some extra sleep and the waking up every morning at the same time thing kind of sucks, well, learn the art of napping. Nobody should have to pull an all day on Sunday. Thing number three is programming. If your programming doesn't make any sense or you haven't looked at it and thought about changing it since you hit a plateau, that's pretty lowhanging fruit and would be one of the first things I would investigate. If you're not running a program at all, then I would recommend you head to calorie barbell.com and download the free 16week program. From there, boom, all your problems are solved. Or you can check out the calorie barbell training app where you'll get access to over 50 programs. You'll get weekly check-ins and coaching from myself and the other Calgary barbell coaches and all of the cool features and UI of an app that's going to track all of your metrics and all of your all the things for you. Not having a plan at all is an incredibly easy thing to solve and provides essentially the baseline for all training decisions. Having a plan, knowing when your bigger and smaller, more important or less important, more demanding or less demanding sessions are, will allow you to be better physically and mentally prepared. Maybe you got to kind of hype yourself up cuz you have a big squat coming up. Or maybe you need to really make sure you get a good sleep on Sunday night cuz Monday's heavy squat day. Without a program, without a plan, all of that is out the window. Thing number four is effort. So, let's talk about effort. And this is not going to be some kind of pseudo macho bootstrap motivational whatever. I in fact want to look at both sides of the coin here. I think that of course there are lifters who are unable or unwilling to be uncomfortable or go in and strain against heavy weights. get up to what would be considered an actual RP8 because newsplash, an RP8 is a hard set. But there are also lifters who go in there and smash their face against the wall, forcing weight onto the bar and calling it an RP7, despite the fact that that set nearly ended their career. So, I want you to take a step back from your own training. Try to see if perhaps your tendencies put you a little far on one end or the other of that spectrum. And if after an honest investigation of the effort you give in the gym, you can say, "Yeah, I've been going way too hard." Or, "Man, I really should learn to try." Then I would say nudge yourself in the direction of the opposite. You might be surprised at how much impact that has moving forward. Thing number five, social comparison. Now, this last one, we're going to kind of flip it on you a little bit. Now, we've been investigating the question of why are you not stronger? And well, maybe you are stronger, but you still feel like about it because X, Y, or Z lifter that you watch on Instagram, or maybe somebody in your gym has gotten stronger faster or is objectively stronger. I want to caution lifters from making these kinds of social comparisons because it can absolutely rob all of the joy from progressing and lifting if that progress isn't as good as another. We're able to do this all of the time with the less than 1% outliers whose progress we can track in real time with the tap of a screen. We're able to make ourselves feel like garbage about the progress that we are making because it's not like theirs. So the next time you're asking yourself, why am I not stronger? Why am I not making any progress? Well, I want you to investigate those five things. Ask yourself, am I eating enough? Am I sleeping and recovering enough? Does my programming make any sense? Am I putting effort in? And am I actually making progress, but just robbing myself of feeling accomplished at all because I'm comparing my progress to others? Go through those five things and I bet you we find some progress. We'll see you in the next one. Peace.

=== FILE: Advanced Squat Progress： Isolation Work Matters Too #powerlifting [OZDgJRdw6wE].en.txt ===

My next piece of advice is to accessorize again but differently. In that last section, we talked about what Bondichuk would call special developmental exercises. And these exercises will target the movement that is the focus of the competitive training. So in the case of the squat, we're looking at things like the pause squat or pin squat. Again, things that target the movement and the pattern. What I want to talk about being important now is what the good doctor would call special preparatory exercises. These are further down the scale of specificity. We're getting into isolation exercises. We're getting into movements that target the muscle as opposed to the movement pattern. As an advanced lifter, you're likely again going to get to a point where there's a bottleneck in how much stress you can put on the body, right? Maybe it's your back or your hips or whatever. But we can't just add squat stress, add infinitum. It just doesn't work like that. What we need to do is come up with creative ways to continue to progressively overload the lifter. If, for example, your bottleneck is your back. Something like a leg press would be a great way to get a lot more training stimulus onto the muscles that can tolerate it and the joints that can tolerate it while getting around the recovery demands of whatever body part or joint doesn't agree to being trained that hard. By choosing appropriate SPE, we can continue to scale training stimulus while being intentional and mindful of our recovery. In conclusion, whatever your milestone is, whatever numbers haunt your dreams or inspire you to keep pushing and going back to the gym, I hope that throughout the course of this, we've given you some advice that is relevant to you and that helps you continue in your journey towards being stronger.

=== FILE: Advice for Your First Powerlifting Meet [JvLmnzAjqDY].en.txt ===

All right, you're doing your first powerlifting competition. You've just come across an eightpart series of hours and hours of information that you feel you need to internalize and get right before this competition. I'm here to tell you that not entirely, but what I'm getting at is that if you're doing your first powerlifting competition, you don't need to get everything right. You don't need to make every single call and put the exact right weight on the bar and and do some kind of advanced water cutting strategy and come in just below your weight class threshold and all this kind of stuff. You just need to go have a good time. Take it a bit conservative. Try and go 9 for9. If you mess up, nobody cares. If you miss weight at a local meet, I don't think there's any rules against just lifting in a different weight class. Most meet directors are not going to care. You're there to get some experience. And if you like it, then you can start layering more complex things on top. But try not to get overly stressed out and anxious about all this massive checklist of stuff that you absolutely have to do. It's your first meet. Just go have a good time. Maybe you make some friends. Maybe bomb out. If you do, that's fine. I bombed out of my second meet. I'm still here.

=== FILE: Be a Good Training Partner #powerlifting [cRRC1ApyqpA].en.txt ===

Hey, you. You go to the gym with your buddy, your group of people. You have training partners, right? Okay, good. Here's how you make the most of those relationships and you push each other to become better at lifting. Now, it's all well and good for you and your training partners to kind of dap each other up after hitting a nice lift and all that kind of stuff, but if you are afraid to hurt your training partner's feelings by saying, "Hey, uh, I think you're squatting high or you're not pausing your benches long enough or, you know, that tempo was dog." Then you're leaving gains on the table because your role as a training partner is about more than just being a hype man. You are there to hold your training partners accountable to ensure that they're lifting to a competition standard. And you don't have to be a about it, but you also should probably say something if you see something. You know what I mean? Help your friends and your training partners become better lifters. Have them do that for you, and you'll be surprised at how many more gains you'll all make.

=== FILE: Build Your Deadlift With Front Squats [PClcOolb9AM].en.txt ===

Okay, this might be a little bit of a hot take, but I honest to God think that the front squat is a great deadlift accessory. I don't think it gets enough credit as a deadlift accessory. And I'll tell you this much, I don't think it's a very good squat accessory. Not for a powerlifter. If you have any training, if you have any strength and ability in the back squat, you've been doing it for a couple years at least, you are not going to get enough weight on a front squat to train your legs that well. Unless you're Jezoa, in which case, go off, king. What I will say though is that the front squat puts the weight in front of you. It forces you to work really hard with your trunk and your upper back musculature to hold that weight stable. And then you do the hinging and pushing with your legs. Does that sound like any other lift? You know, maybe the deadlift. So, if you've tried every other accessory movement to try to blow your deadlift up and none of them seem to be working and uh you know, maybe you're feeling like taking a risk, throw in some front squats, work them, see if it helps your deadlift. Don't be surprised if it does. And if you want to know four other of my favorite accessory movements, you can head over to our YouTube channel and check out the video we just did where I go over my five favorite deadlift accessories. Hint, I already gave you

=== FILE: Chasing a 405 Bench？ Less Might Be More. #powerlifting [tCwZLSXxB5Y].en.txt ===

And now we come to the last boss of bench press, at least for a lot of people, 405. All right, so coming up against the more advanced milestone that you've set for yourself, whether that's 405 or whatever, here are some sort of final tips to push you past that level of ascension to help you level up into your final form, unlock your final class, and evolve into the Charizard that you were born to be. All right. So, my first tip here, I know I talked a lot more about benching more to bench more and then benching more than more and blah blah blah, but now I'm going to flip it on you because sometimes less is more. When you get to these advanced stages of lifting, sometimes you need even more to separate out the work in terms of where you can actually afford to push hard, how frequently you can afford to push hard, how much of your volume is going to be split between the competition lift and even very non-specific accessories like direct tricep work or cable flies and things like that. Yes, we need progressive overload. Yes, we probably need more stimulus to get to 405 than we did to get to 315. But if we try to do it the exact same way and just hammer the bench pattern itself, we might be missing out on gains and we may also just end up overtraining and injuring ourselves.

=== FILE: DEADLIFT TIPS & TRICKS [rzyWGRAb4dU].en.txt ===

You like that, eh? Yeah, me too. Hi guys, Bryce here from Calgary Barbell again. Uh, today we're going to do a little deadlift tutorial. I'm going to run through the conventional deadlift specifically cuz that's how I pull and uh we're going to go through some of the steps that I use when I deadlift and uh go from there. My biggest deadlift in competition was 756 lbs. uh 343 kilos and that was at the recent North American Championships. So when I deadlift, there's about four steps that I go through. The first one's going to be the setup. Second's going to be bracing the torso. Third is going to be pulling into tension at the bottom. That one's really important and often overlooked. And the fourth is the actual pull itself. First thing I'll do when I approach the bar is get my feet set. So what I generally like to do is be pretty much straight down from my hips. That's going to allow all your joints to be nice and stacked. That should in theory support the most weight. Bigger guys, bigger thighs, might need to go a little wider. But another thing you really need to take into consideration with your setup is how wide your grip's going to have to be to accommodate what your knees need to be doing. What I like to do is I like to take my my breath at the top. So, this is going to be going into bracing. Now, what you'll see me do is sort of lock my lats down, get my breath for my first rep before I go down to the bar. especially with a belt on, this helps me get a little more air in. The third step that's really, really important that a lot of people overlook is to pull yourself into tension. So, what you need to do is you're going to take your grip now that you're nice and braced and you're going to pull on the bar with your lats. You're going to allow your knees to travel forward a little bit. You're going to sit your butt down until you feel tension in your whole back through your core, your quads, your glutes, and your hamstrings. So basically your entire body is already firing at this point. Being that tight is going to make sure you have a good pull. So the next thing is the actual deadlift itself. The pull. Now a lot of people are going to have a different starting point. Some people are going to start their hips a little higher, some people a little lower. It's going to depend on leverages and limb lengths and strengths and weaknesses and all that stuff. But we do need to make sure that we stay in a similar position that we start in. So the first phase of the deadlift off the floor should be pretty much straight up. So you're not letting your hips shoot up. Your hip angle's not changing. It's kind of like a leg press. You're going to think about pushing the floor away more so than starting to pull back. If you start to pull back too early, your knees are going to go forward and you're going to be pulling against yourself, essentially making lift way harder than it should be. So straight up off the floor. Once you pass the knees, you're going to think about squeezing your glutes and driving your hips forward. and at the same time pulling back with your lats. As you get to the top of the lift, depending on what federation you're in, uh they're going to be a little sticky. You got to make sure you lock your knees out. Um but that's it.

=== FILE: Deadlift Hip Height： Get It Right Every Time! [y3wuEZ-lKTY].en.txt ===

I've coached and known lifters over the years whose first rep of a set of deadlifts is the hardest now you'd think the first rep of the set should be the easiest and the smoothest rep however in the case of the deadlift there are certainly exceptions to that rule if this is an issue you're dealing with in your training today's video is going to be my attempt at explaining it and presenting some options to help you solve it because especially if you're a power lifter we only get the first rep hold on now before we go down the rabbit hole of my complex explanations and mechanistic reasons why this might be happening and I present you with the solutions I realize I'm making a bit of an assumption and my assumption here is that you're not doing touch and go deadlifts that you're not bouncing the bar between reps if you are doing touch and go deadlifts and your first rep of your set is the hardest stop it fully reset the bar between reps stop doing touch and go deadlifts and watch your deadlift go up now back to the let's take a look at the reasons that this might be happening as best I can tell to come to mind the first reason would be that your start position on rep one is worse and different and the second reason is not being able to fully brace or exert force on that first rep now we're going to start with number one and assume that the start position is the issue because it's the first rep of the set the lifter has all the Time in the World to try and set the perfect start position however sometimes this leads the athlete to overthink and then over wedge themselves and what I mean by over wedge is that the lifter is setting their hips too low they're setting their torso too upright and due to that ending up with their shoulder blade and too much of the mass of their body behind the bar now when we try to start a pull from this position we're actually working against ourselves we're pulling back because of the line of pull to the shoulder blades but we're pulling back through our Shins which is going to make the lift drastically more difficult we also don't get nearly as much posterior chain involvement when we're overly pulled into the bar like this and it leads to a very squatty deadlift now if you're sitting there wondering that might be me but how the heck am I gonna know well let me take you through how you would diagnose this all you'll need to do for this is simply film a set of your deadlifts with a weight That's Heavy enough for the issue to show up you're going to want to film it straight on from a side angle and try to get a freeze frame of exactly when you start the deadlift now a more advanced trick here would be use some sort of pen tool on your monitor to Mark the shoulder blades and your hip and knee positions in your first rep and then let it play through to the second rep and see if things line up with the reference points if you don't have a pen tool and you don't want to go through all that work you should be able to just look at the screenshots and see if there's a noticeable difference between the two starting points so if you can notice that your start position is definitely different from first to subsequent reps then here's what you can do firstly I would say the skills method practice practice and practice play around with tension and sensation in your hips your hamstrings your quads and your feet and try to recreate that better position that you're in from reps to and onwards think about what it feels like to be in that position and practice getting into it frequently now if you want you can practice pulling his attention every time you go to the gym just put a little bit of weight on the bar enough that you can pull some tension and slack out and pull yourself into that position over and over again you can do sets of this and you don't even have to actually do the deadlift part it's more important that we practice the position now the other way to address this is going to be through programming you want to choose exercises that are going to allow you a better opportunity to go through the start position and the earlier phase of the lift more often here's a few of my personal recommendations my first recommendation is going to be the paused deadlift you're going to initiate the lift as normal taking special care to make sure you have a good start position you're going to pause the bar about one inch off the floor hold for one or two count and then go through to completion of the lift my second recommendation is going to be the double or triple start deadlift so you're gonna again pay very close attention to your start position but you're going to initiate the lift bring the bar to the knees set it back down initiate the lift again and go through to completion that would be a double start deadlift and for the Triple start you're going to do the false start pulling the bar to your knees twice before your full rep and my final recommendation is the tempo eccentric deadlift now I will give a caveat this is probably going to work better for a conventional puller than a Sumo puller but for those who struggle with start position setting the bar down slowly from the top is going to help you find a really good start position where you set the bar down to take note of your positioning as the bar reaches the floor and that's probably going to be a really good start position if you check your start positions and you don't see a notable difference then you're probably running into this issue as a result of our reason number two which is not producing enough tension or exerting enough force on the first rep of your deadlift so in order to explain this I'm gonna get a bit theoretical now bear in mind that this is all just my own conjecture so take it with a grain of salt there's this thing called henneman's size principle and it states that motor neurons are recruited in order of size from smallest to largest and the way this relates back to the topic at hand is that I think those lifters who struggle with that first rep and then are performing better on subsequent reps I think they're struggling with a timely recruitment of the muscles and the motor neurons responsible for bracing and responsible for moving the larger muscles that take care of the range of motion of the deadlift so regardless of whether my pseudoscience explanation as to The last question you want to ask yourself is, can you afford it? Do you have the additional resources to commit to paying for a coach? You know, I'm a fan of the adage that, like tattoos, good coaches aren't cheap and cheap coaches aren't good, at least generally speaking. So if the idea of getting coached sounds like something you're interested in, if you have big goals and would like to accomplish lots and accelerate your road to accomplishing those things and you have the finances to do so, you're probably a good candidate for a coach. So what can you expect and what are the benefits of having a coach? Like I said, one of the main benefits of hiring a coach is obviously making more progress, right? You're going to put kilos on your total, gain muscle, lose fat, whatever your goals are, coaches are there to speed you along your way. Another thing that I think is really important in a good coaching relationship is it allows you peace of mind. A good coaching relationship is going to be centered around trust and your trust that the coach is implementing the correct and optimal strategies to give you the results that you're after, thereby giving you peace of mind to trust that you're doing the right thing at the right time. And I think to some extent, even just that buy-in of feeling like whatever I'm doing, it's the right thing. Whether or not you are somebody who wants to be involved in the coaching process and has input and questions about the programming and the philosophy underpinning the programming, having a coach gives you somebody to turn to when things aren't going correctly. If we're not making the progress that we desire, a good coach is going to have a way to iterate and adapt, making changes to things so that you can course correct or they'll be able to, you know, assuage your concerns and say, that's all right. Now, with all that being said, for the sake of balanced discussion, let's play devil's advocate a little bit and talk about those who maybe shouldn't get a coach or who might not benefit so much from that coaching relationship. If you are someone who really struggles with sort of handing over the reins to your training, if you're someone who enjoys and benefits from the freedom to be able to go in and change stuff on the fly, sometimes not even doing the programming that you've written for yourself, but rather adopting things wholesale based on whatever metrics you might have for making those changes, if that method of doing things is something that you enjoy and something that is productive for you, then I see no reason to change that system. Now, there are certainly some instances where if you're program hopping or changing everything as soon as you get into the gym and not sticking to your plan, maybe that's a strong indication that you should have a coach, but there are those who enjoy that and benefit from that. And when it comes to the communication, you know, if you're somebody who wants a little more of a guiding hand, do they do weekly check-ins? I think another important thing in this sort of cost assessment is going to be being able to commit to probably 10 or 12 weeks to actually try a coach out. It can be easy in some instances to bounce off of a coaching relationship if those first few weeks aren't great. So what I'm saying is budget for a decent little bit of time if you're going to start with a new coach to make your assessment. That being said, there are certainly some things to watch out for with a new coach. Some red flags, if you will. As part of this process, I would also reach out to some lifters that have been coached by the coach before or lifters who are currently being coached. I would probably try to get a sample of both. Now let's say you get started with a coach. What should you expect? What are the green flags of coaching? So once you've begun with a coach, you should expect the following things. Number one, getting your programming on time. This is the absolute lowest bar to set. This is showing up for work as a powerlifting coach. You know, I'm human. There have been instances where programming has been late but if this is a chronic thing or if it doesn't show up for multiple days or a week, that is problematic. At a base with any coach, you should get your programming. Number two, responsiveness. I think a lot of people see coaching as programming but programming is programming and coaching is communication. It is education. It is listening. It is being able to reflect on other people's perspectives. Being able to collaborate and being able to contextualize sometimes subtle hints in communication in order to do a better job for people. So, you know, again, you should expect some level of communication and responsiveness. Number three, a why. Even if it isn't the most optimal training program for you, you buying into it and believing it's going to work give you much greater odds of success in that program. And number four, meaningful feedback. Not just feedback but meaningful feedback. This one can be a little bit tricky because I think sometimes, you know, if I get a new lifter who comes to me and their squat is excellent, it's progressing, it's comfortable, it's repeatable, their technique is like I said consistent, I'm not going to change it. I think in some instances it may be sort of a fear on the coach's part that if they don't offer feedback or maybe a perception of the clients that if they don't get feedback other than looks good that they're not getting value but in some cases withholding that feedback and just saying hey, you're doing a great job, keep doing this is the feedback that people need. Now, on the flip side, if that's the only feedback you get is that hey, this looks good, let's go up five pounds but the video you sent them was you missing a lift, well, I think at that point you should be getting more feedback than that. So, there's a sweet spot in between, right, where you're going to get responses and feedback on things that are relevant and things that are helpful but not necessarily just changing things for changing things' sake. So, if you feel like the feedback you're getting is meaningful and actionable and it's being given in a way where you have the freedom to have some say in it, I think that's a really important thing. And number five, my last point here is collaboration. I think that any coaching relationship should be a two-way street. I don't have a single lifter that I just tell them what they're going to do and that's it. Most things should be a conversation. Most things should involve feedback and potentially retooling strategies or selecting different exercises. I think that lifters having agency in their programming is really important because again, this all feeds back, if you haven't noticed, by now, this all feeds back into the buy-in concept. This all feeds back into believing in your training and thinking and knowing that it's going to work. And if your coach took that idea you had to try pin squats this block and your squat blows up, I mean, you're both happy at that point. Your coach shouldn't be fragile enough that you having a good idea is threatening somehow to them. A collaborative effort is always going to be preferable. There are points where, you know, a coach, if they have a good reason to say no, they should say no. They should also be able to put their foot down in some instances. But, if they don't have a good reason to say no, they should probably be open to at least talking to you and being reasonable with your feedback in your training. if you're having troubles with your deadlift grip and you're unwilling to send your thumbs to the shadow Realm by hook gripping you might be making this one mistake so let's see if we can fix it the first mistake a lot of people make in a mix grip when they know they might drop the bar maybe they don't have the best grip is they're going to overgrip it so they're going to go down they're going to wrap half their freaking hand around the bar their wrists are going to be all bent and then look what happens as soon as I pick it up right my wrists need to go back to straight they're G to hang down that is just going to happen if you're over gripping like that the first thing that happens when you're putting force and exerting yourself against the weight of the bar is that bar is already slipping out of your hands that is not going to be good for your grip so what I recommend is to take the bar instead of way up here in your hand take it a little further down here now hear me out if you take the bar further down you want your wrists to be straight through because again that's just where they're going to go unless you can wrist curl your deadlift in which case I mean I don't know I I got nothing left to teach you but uh if you have the bar Lower in your fingers it's going to feel like maybe it's a bit less secure but it's actually going to be able to test your grip strength if you gripped a bar like that in training you're going to be able to train your grip strength as opposed to having to train your grip strength and use your grip against a rolling bar so stop gripping the bar up here and thinking that wedging half your hand meat underneath it is going to hold on to it put it further down in your fingers use your grip train your grip and it'll get better

=== FILE: Fix Your Bar Position for a Stronger Squat [KOK4LfTtGyk].en.txt ===

We're gonna go through how to get the bar into the right position on your back. Now, this is something that seems simple. I think a lot of people sort of intuitively figure it out, but there are those who struggle with it. So, if that's you, let's fix your shelf, which will help fix your brace and help make your squat better. We'll talk a little bit about grip width and some of the stuff you can do there. But first, I want to tackle the big thing, which is just where does the gar Oh, hello. where does the bar go on your back? So, whatever your chosen grip is, again, we'll talk about that in a sec. Get under the bar with your hands on it and and touch it to your traps, right? Just below your neck. Basically, all you're going to do from here is slide the bar down by pushing yourself further under until it kind of just stops. There should be a spot just below your traps where it feels like it kind of slots in, right? It's going to be just on top of your rear delts. From that position, you should be able to stand the bar up. And I think another mistake a lot of people make is when they're standing the bar up and walking it out, they're trying to be super upright and they're like, "Wow, the bar's falling off me." Yeah, it's going to do that. If the bar's in a good place, you're going to need to have, you can see this like little bit of hinge, right? this little bit of break in the hips so that the bar is straight up and down into your upper back as opposed to falling off of your back. If your hips are all the way locked through, yes, it's going to fall off your back. And I think what a lot of people mistakenly do is they try to be really upright and then they just do this with their shoulders to make the bar stay on their back and not fall off. When in actuality, we want those shoulders pulled down onto the rib cage. We just need that little bit of a tilt to keep it where it's going to go. Now, there are a whole bunch of different things going to be really individual from from lifter to lifter, right? So, one of them is going to be width. You tend to see bigger lifters from 105 and up on the men's side. And I think women's side is a lot more varied in grip position. You tend to see bigger lifters a little more out wide, right? maybe first finger on the rings or even wider just to make room for the fact that they have broad shoulders getting under the bar. You tend to see lighter weight lifters in closer and tighter. I do think it's worth noting that there's a grip narrowness that I think is into diminishing returns. Right. Generally, the tighter we go in here, the tighter we're going to be able to get the upper back. But if we get too tight, it's just going to stuff everything in there and we won't be able to actually pull ourselves in, right? We won't be able to actually set the upper back and create that tension cuz it's just kind of too tight. It's already there. The next thing I'm going to talk about is thumbs behind versus thumbs around the bar. In my federation, that's the only options. We can't do any of this kind of stuff. If you're in an untested federation or nonIPF or your federation allows this, a lot of people will put their pinky around the bar like this. And in some cases, it tends to relieve a little bit of elbow and shoulder discomfort if you have that. Unfortunately, in the IPF, we've got these two options, right? So, if you're having wrist, elbow, shoulder junkiness, number one, look at the shoulders and make sure you're not doing this because if that shoulder moves forwards, right, it makes everything more forwards. It pulls this wrist and hand and whole arm forwards, which means it's going to take more tension to get it behind the bar. Step number one, if we're having wrist, elbow, shoulder stuff, is pull those shoulders back and down. to make sure that we're not compensating for standing super upright by being shrugged and forward in the shoulders. Then we can look at thumbs around versus thumbs over, grip width, wider, narrower. I actually used to go wider when I was lighter. Contrary to what I was saying earlier, I found when I got bigger and moved up a weight class from 105 to 120, moving my grip in was really helpful. I think because it was better for me to put the stress on my wrists and elbows as opposed to my shoulders. I found that out wide here, it was more stress on my shoulders. They got more beat up. Coming in narrower, a little more stress on my wrists and elbows and they were able to tolerate it. Through all of that, I hope that you have an idea of how to get the bar where it needs to be, what our sort of unrackck should be like, what some of the common faults are with bar positioning, and some of the things you can play with if you're struggling. If you have other questions, if you have fixed yourself using some cool tricks, let us know in the comments below. Leave a like if you liked it. Hit that subscribe button. If you're having a really distinct sticking point halfway through your bench or you're getting super stuck off the chest, you might be messing up your elbow position. === FILE: Fix Your Foot Pressure for a Stronger Squat [yKzwUotaK-w].en.txt ===

Mistake number five, incorrect foot pressure. Now, incorrect foot pressure is a bit vague in general, but that's because it covers a few different faults. So, let's talk about some of the more common issues. Probably the most common issue with incorrect foot pressure is when lifters rock too far forwards on their feet in the bottom of the squat. A lot of these lifters are very self-aware. They know they have a tendency of falling forwards. And part of the issue is that they're trying to fix that before they start the squat by being way far back on their heels. When these lifters are so far back on the heels, they are inevitably going to have to shift their center of mass forwards when they hit depth. This is going to cause them to pop much more far forwards than they'd like. And the fix for these lifters is to actually start with a little more pressure on the fronts of their feet. If you have this issue and you can start with a more balanced foot pressure, thinking about finding pressure both on the ball of your feet and the heels before you start and then just work to maintain that throughout the squat. Tempo squats can be kind of helpful there just so you can feel out each of the positions as you move through. The next common issue with foot pressure is when lifters end up on the insides of their feet. Now, this one often coincides with sliding or popping forwards at the bottom, but it's also usually a symptom of being perhaps too wide in the stance and too towed outwards. If you're a lifter who falls onto the insides of their feet in the bottom of the squat, my first place that I recommend you look at making changes is going to be in your stance width and your toe angle. Generally speaking, these lifters should narrow their stance up, even if just slightly, and bring their toe angle a little more towards straight forwards. This can help just allow the knees to track where they want to based on your hip strength and anatomy instead of forcing yourself into a position where you then have to change it to produce force on the way

=== FILE: Fix Your Squat With Pin Squats #powerlifting #squats [VgacWpTheBY].en.txt ===

The second movement that we're going to talk about is the pin squat. Now, the pin squat is going to expose any weaknesses you have out of your bottom position. It forces you to maintain some tension to the bar, but also forces you to delo some of that tension. It's it's about finding sort of a perfect balance between how much you're unloading onto the pins. The reason this is so good is that if you have any issues coming out of the bottom in terms of holding your torso position, if your quads or your hips are not strong enough for you to come up without compromising that position, your hips shooting up, your knees caving a whole bunch, those kinds of things, do pin squats. Because if you have those issues, you're going to be terrible at pin squats. And getting better at pin squats means getting better at those positions, which should then carry over to your comp squat and make you better. Okay. So, the the the Ps to a good pin squat, the key to good pin squats is going to be finding the right pin height. So, if you go a little bit high and your squat is a little bit high to pins, that's fine. Make sure that when you're going down to the pins, however, a lot of people will kind of keep their hips high and then fold down to meet with their trunk. We want to make sure we're getting all the same depth in the hips. Reach back. And then when we come off the pins, a lot of people are going to end up getting this. They're going to start losing position because it's going to be really hard to keep your quads engaged and to stay in the position we want out at the bottom. That's where we're really going to be tested. So, if we find the right height and we're able to drive the knees forward out of the bottom, we shouldn't see too much of that hips shooting up and then that's going to fix that in your comp squat. One last thing, don't go crashing onto the pins. It doesn't have to be light as a feather, but we don't want you to just get halfway down and then free fall to the pins and try to start from a dead stop. You want to maintain at least some control of the bar throughout the entirety of the movement. The bar should never completely unload on the pins.

 vststst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst vst v with deadlift grip is, is to keep the bar from rolling. Now, the first big tip is to take the bar lower in your hand. A lot of people think that if they put the bar really high up in their hand, kind of like how we talked about in the bench grip, sorry, that there's going to be more meat of the hand to wrap around it, that that's going to be sturdier. However, in my experience and in working with athletes, the big thing that I find is that bar is going to roll to the end of your grip as soon as you start deadlifting. Now, if that bar is really high up, that's going to tear calluses. It's going to create again, that momentum moving in the opposite direction. We're trying to pull the bar. So what my recommendation here is, is to take that bar lower along these knuckles here, almost in the fingertips so that when we start, that bar is already set and it's not going to roll any further. The next big thing that kind of piggybacks on that last idea is to pull the slack out of your grip. Now, we talked recently in a deadlift video about pulling the slack out of the bar to make sure that we had tension set into the bar. We want to make sure the same thing's happening with your grip so that again, even putting it lower in your hands, we want to make sure that we're pulled to the end of the grip before we initiate the lift and put everything into trying to break that bar off the floor. Again, if there's any roll, it's going to work against you. Very similarly in hook grip, we'll notice that a lot of people will set that hook grip very deep, which is fine. We can get a little bit more grip on the thumb, but we want to make sure that by the time we start that pull, we're down towards the end of where that bar is going to end up. Now, it might seem a little bit riskier, but again, we want to reduce that bar rolling. And lastly, just a little bit of a tip for those who choose to hook grip or who are having trouble learning the hook grip. Now, honestly, the first time I tried to hook grip, what I did was just wrap my thumb around the bar like I normally would and then try to jam my fingers on top of it. Now, that's not bad, but one thing that I actually learned from Clint Darden when I first started getting into using hook grip was to lay the thumb as parallel to the bar as possible so that you have more length of the thumb to grab onto. Now, the big thing here is that we want the middle finger to dig right into that dent just below the thumbnail and the first finger to just kind of grab on wherever you can. Now, you'll notice if you look at any of my heavy deadlifts that I've hook gripped, these two fingers, my ring finger, my pinky finger, are barely even on the bar. They don't really have much to do with it. They're almost under the bar at that point. So they're just kind of along for the ride. The big thing is going to be getting as much of these first two fingers wrapped around that thumb as you can. And by laying the thumb parallel to the bar, as opposed to perpendicular, we're going to get a lot more to grab onto. Hopefully, this video helps everybody to make more deadlifts, to drop less of them, and to keep that damn bar from rolling out of your hands. === FILE: HOW TO BENCH PRESS [w0XBfuCC2WM].en.txt ===

And that, my friends, is the bench press. What's going on, guys? We are here at Calgary Barbell. We've been asked a couple times now to film some other lift tutorials like we did with the deadlift. So, what we're going to do today is we're going to go through the bench press. Now, the way I break it down is I have five sort of segments to it. So, the first is going to be your setup, and it's of the utmost importance. The next thing is going to be the unrackck, which is something I feel people often overlook. The next is going to be the descent. The fourth is going to be the pause or the chest position position on your chest rather. And the fifth is going to be the actual press. First things first, we need to get set up for the bench press. The way you set yourself up sets the tone for the rest of the lift. So, make sure we're doing it right. The first thing I do is I set my grip. I find once I'm connected to the bar, once my grip's set, I can actually use the weight of the bar a little bit, pushing and pulling to help me set my shoulders. We're not going to talk too much about grip width because that's something that's going to be uh very different from person to person and something that I can't necessarily give you any hard and fast rules for. So, you're going to have to find your own grip width, but I will give you some tips on how to grip the bar. So, for myself, I like to take the bar low in the palm. So, you see a lot of people take the bar what I feel is too high in the palm. Now, that's going to end up putting the bar back behind the wrist and generally the elbows are going to get overtucked. You can end up with some issues in terms of wrist and elbow tendonitis in the long term. Uh, and you can also end up in just a poor position for pressing. So, to get set, I lay down and I'll actually take a little bit of an internally rotated grip to get that weight in the right part of my palms where I like it. I'll grab the bar and then I'll kind of crank in. So, my wrists are now more uh more neutral as opposed to internally rotated at the at the shoulder. So, we'll set the grip and then I'll actually push it back into the rack. Then, I'll pop up to set the upper back next. When I'm setting my upper back, I'll scooch myself down the bench towards my feet. Then, I pull the shoulders together and then push from my feet, keeping the shoulders together to drive the shoulders down. So, there's the two biggest things we want to think about in our shoulders is pulling them together and then pulling them down towards your butt. When you're in the right spot, you should feel most of the pressure of your body weight at this point on your upper traps. Then, what you want to do, set your butt down, keeping your shoulders tight. You see a lot of people go like this and then everything flattens out. You've just essentially sabotaged your own setup. So, shoulders pulled in. Push up to drive the shoulders down. Keep them tight as you set your butt down. At this point, I'm pulling on the bar to tighten my lats and drive my chest up as I set my butt down. Then, I'll set my feet. For myself, I'm trying to get my feet back a little further cuz I had some issues with my butt coming up off the bench at my last meet. So, there we're essentially set up. So, the next thing I want to talk about with the setup is going to be leg drive. I try to maintain consistent leg drive, pushing me this way towards my head up the bench to keep me on my traps, to keep me in position, to keep my chest up, limit the range of motion, all that good stuff. You'll see a lot of people sink into their chest a little bit and use leg drive to kind of bump the bar back uh to get the press started. I don't advocate that because I find unless you're really advanced and you've been using that technique for years and years, um it can lead to some pretty inconsistent presses because you essentially have to get the right amount of leg drive to put the bar in the right place and then catch it at the right point to press through and follow through. Once we're set up is we need to unrackck the bar. So, there's a couple mistakes I think people make here. The first one is getting loose as you unrackck. So, there's a couple different ways that people do that. either we'll roll the shoulders out and then come out or we'll press too hard or press too much out of the rack so that it jolts things and we're essentially losing the tension from the setup. Most importantly here is you maintain the tension from your setup to get the bar into position. That's the objective here. So you'll notice when I unrackck my bench press breath just triceps unrackcked. It's just enough to clear the hooks and then we pull the bar into position. That's the next thing I'm going to talk about is pulling the bar into position. Essentially, what we're trying to do is we're trying to move the bar down the body to the point where the lats start to engage, the shoulder blades sink even further from their setup position, and it drives the chest up and forces as much extension as we can get through the upper back. You'll know this because you'll be able to feel your lats start to contract, your back will get tighter, and uh the bar will start to feel almost almost weightless in that point, like you could kind of hold it there for as long as you want it. So, I'll show you an example of what my unrackck looks like. So, we're set up. Big air. Pop with the triceps. Pull into position. So, the next thing we're going to talk about is the descent of the bar to your chest. The two major points here that I want to make note of are going to be where the elbows are tracking and where you're touching on your chest. So, with the elbow tracking, we essentially want a nice stacked position. Hence the position we took with the bar in our hand. We want a nice stack position through the wrist, through the elbow. You'll see a lot of people overtuck or undertuck, uh, meaning too much or too little external rotation in the shoulder. And that's going to put you in a position where you're straining some of the supporting muscles or you're just not going to have a lot of power. We always want nice stacked joints. Now, you're going to get to a certain point in the lowering phase where you're going to start to feel a lot of tension across the chest. And what a lot of people do incorrectly is they dodge the tension and they dump lower. Now again, this goes back to that sink and heave versus constant tension kind of bench press. For the constant tension crowd, we're going to want to pull down. When we get to that point of tension, we essentially want to try to drive the shoulders back further, bring the chest up further, and lower the bar as little as possible, but pulling the bar in. We want to be actively almost rowing the bar to the chest. That last little bit of range of motion. So very very strong back contraction driving the chest up to meet the bar keeping everything nice and tight all the way to the chest. So again, setup, grip, upper back, butt down, feet planted, unrackck. We're going to have breath, pull into position. Now lowering phase. Elbows stay under the bar. Find the tension. Pull in. Back is tight as crap. And it's cramping and I can't hold it. But that's the kind of tension you want. to show you guys what we don't want to do. I'm going to set up again. Okay. Now, so if you come down, we're starting to feel tension around here and a lot of people will touch lower and then we sort of lose it. Bars out in front of the elbows and we have to do a little bit of a almost a front delt raise to get the bar back in a position and press through. We want the press to stay a press. We don't want it to turn into a front delt raise. So, we need to load up the pecs and press. The very last phase of the lift is going to be the press itself. If we were to press straight up from the touch point on the chest without bringing it back over the shoulder, we're going to end up out in front of the shoulder. We're going to have significantly worse leverage down there. So, what we want to do is we essentially want to bring the bar back over the shoulders as the first part of the press and then we want to press straight through to lock out. One of the mistakes I see people make with the the pressing back over the shoulders movement is I see people press back over the shoulders, but then the bar continues back up over the face kind of thing. So, we end up in this position where we're totally internally rotated. The shoulder blades have lost their position from the setup and you're not in a good position should you need to do more reps. So, the bar path we're looking for is to the chest, back over the shoulder and up. To the chest, back over the shoulder and up. What we don't want is to the chest back over the shoulder back. As you can see, wildly out of control there. The other thing we don't want is down and press out because again, we're losing leverage there. So, with the last portion of the lift, with the lockout, the biggest thing we want to be conscious of is still maintaining position. We want to be keeping those shoulder blades in position throughout the entirety of the lift. We don't want to be getting to the top, locking the the triceps, and then having the shoulders follow through. Again, especially if we're doing more reps. Less important on a single as long as we get the lift, but more important on a set of reps cuz if we get to the top, we lose position in the shoulders, we're going to be screwed for our next rep. So, the biggest thing that I think about to help me ensure that my lockout is stays tight is to just lock with the triceps. So, we get to the top, keep the shoulders in position, squeeze the triceps to lock out. That's going to straighten the elbows. You're going to get those white lights from the judges, and it's going to prevent your shoulders from popping out behind the bar and screwing you up for your next rep. So, that's it for the bench press. If you have any questions, if there's anything I didn't cover or you want to know more about, feel free to ask in the comments below. Make sure to hit that like button, share with your friends, and subscribe if you haven't already. Thanks for tuning in, guys.

=== FILE: How Proper Bracing Makes Squat Depth Easier #powerlifting [hcTIg_Q9Bbg].en.txt ===

Proper bracing in our squat is going to look like more of a neutral range back position. We're queuing the lifter to kind of pull the ribs down, tuck the pelvis in maybe a little bit. More on that later, but we're trying to achieve something that looks more similar to the bottom position. Even if you brace properly, there's going to be a slight change in your low back and pelvis position to get depth. But we're working to try to minimize that change so that you don't feel as much of a big loss of position and you can be more consistent with your torso and your bracing throughout the entirety of the squat.

of the dynamic nature of doing it this way lifters will need to put in practice to master this jolt style of leg drive to ensure that they can be consistent with it alright now that we've covered all bar and I would do this lightly don't ruin a block of chalk for this so I could see exactly where the bar touched each and every rep with the goal being a single chalk Mark at the end of the set another major component of the touch is the weight of the touch and what I mean by this is how hard or lightly you touch the bar to your chest a good way to think about it is in terms of the hands and 10 to 20 percent unloading on my chest in the bottom position touch weight will also have a fair a bit to do with your leg Drive style which we covered a lot of in the last video but for those lifters using more sinking and a heavier touch the jolt style of lag Drive is usually preferred where lifters with a lighter touch and more weight in the hands we'll often use a more consistent shoulder joints what we're looking at when referees are judging the top of the shoulder joint is actually going to be be the top of the shoulder joint if the lifter were standing so we're looking at elbow is parallel to or below the center of your shoulder joint when you're lying down and the head referee is looking straight on at you then you are fulfilling the requirement of bench depth now
