=== FILE: How to Choose the Right Attempts on Meet Day (and Actually Hit Them) [kEEhyzlkdoE].en.txt ===

A powerlifting competition is the ultimate test of strength, but you only have three attempts per lift to show what you're capable of. So, how do you choose attempts on the day to ensure that you do just that? In today's video, we'll give you the ins and outs of attempt selection. We'll be referencing the meat card that we used in our last video. So, if you don't have a copy of that yet, check down in the description box below so that you can follow along. When it comes to our attempt selection, I like to start by coming up with a good goal for your third attempt. Here's what that looks like. Obviously, your third attempt is going to be 100%. Your second attempt is going to be somewhere in the neighborhood of 95 96% and your opening attempt is going to be somewhere around 90 to 92%. So, this is a great start for an approximate plan, but keep in mind that everything can change and in some cases should change. My biggest piece of advice when it comes to attempt selection is do not be married to the numbers. How aggressive or conservative you are with attempts will have a lot to do with your goals for the day. Whether you're trying to qualify for a further competition, whether you're trying to compete head-to-head directly against another opponent, or whether you're there to just hit some PRs and have fun. If it's your first competition and you're just feeling out what powerlifting is like as a sport, then you're probably going to want to be a bit more conservative with your attempt selection. If you have a head-to-head direct competitor or you're looking for a qualifying total, then you have a decent reason to push harder and be slightly more aggressive with your attempts. Speaking of records, here's Ry Stin with an unofficial world record bench press of 229 kilos. Now, wouldn't you want to get your bench press equipment from somebody who knew what the heck they were talking about? If you're like me and would prefer to source things from someone who lives and breathes the sport, make sure to check out our video sponsors at innerstrengthproducts.ca. The company's owned by Rhea and her husband, Ryan Stin, and they're based here in Canada. They have an incredible selection of products, and they'll take care of all of your powerlifting needs. With that out of the way, let's go through our attempts in a sort of playbyplay. First, you're going to head up into the tunnel or staging area. When you're maybe two to three lifters out, you're going to wait for the call that the bar is loaded. Then, you'll head out onto the platform. When the head ref yells, "Bar is loaded," you have one minute to get the start command in the case of the squat or bench. And in the case of the deadlift, you have that same one minute to start lifting the bar. Quick tip, if you're handling or coaching, make sure as your lifter goes out to double check the screen as well as the weight on the bar and the rack height. Make sure these things are correct, and if there's any mistakes there, you can notify the head referee to have it corrected. Next, you'll proceed to the platform and perform the lift as per the commands we discussed in video number three. As you walk off the platform, lights will come up indicating whether your lift was successful or whether it wasn't. Each of these lights that comes up after your lift represents one of the three referees. A white light means they approve your lift and it is successful if you have a majority of white lights, two or three. And a red light means that that referee does not believe you fulfilled the requirements of a successful lift. A failed lift is two or three red lights. Once these lights come up, you have 1 minute to submit your next attempt to the scoring table. If you failed to submit your next attempt in time, one of two things will happen. Number one, if you made your lift, then failed to submit, you're going to get an increase of 2.5 kilos for your next attempt. Number two, if you failed your lift, then failed to submit, you'll repeat that weight on your next attempt. You should have a pretty good idea of the jump you want to make from first to second attempt because you have this handy dandy meat card that you filled out ahead of time. So now all that's left is making the call. That call being whether you take the jump to your planned second attempt or you shoot a bit lower. For anyone familiar with RPE, I would say an opening attempt at an RP 7 to 7.5 indicates let's take the full jump. For anyone maybe less familiar or unfamiliar completely with RP, a 7 to 7.5 would be indicated by a really smooth lift and the absence of any distinguishable sticking point. Now, let's reference our two potential strategies. both a strategy that's a little bit more aggressive and risky and a strategy that's a little bit more conservative and playing it safe. In our aggressive scenario, you are looking for a qualifying total or going head-to-head with a competitor. In this case, it's almost always better to take the planned jump or very close to, which is often about 6% of the bar load. If your second attempt is a little bit too hard, you can always take a smaller jump to your third. But it's very hard to take a small jump to second. Realize, hm, I'm stronger than I thought I was, and then take a really big jump. Hail Mary, swing for the fences on your third. In the conservative scenario, if this is your first competition and maybe you're feeling a bit nervous or anxious about the bar weights on the day, firstly, this is where having a handler or a coach or somebody who knows you're lifting and ideally knows the sport of powerlifting a little bit comes in very handy. If you're on your own and the sheets calling for a 6% jump that you just don't think is there, feel free to lower that to a 3 to 5% jump. A good tip when it comes to planning your attempts out and taking that jump from first to second is I would almost always rather see a bigger jump from first to second than from second to third attempt. Let's say that you're trying to make a 20 kilo spread between your opening attempt and your final attempt. You might look at that and think, let's go from opener 10 kilos up to second and then we go 10 kilos from second to third. Because of the fact it gets harder to predict your strength once we get heavier and closer to the limit, I would almost always rather take the bigger jump first and instead go 12.5 to second attempt and 7.5 to third attempt. Now, once you've done your second attempt, we should have a pretty good idea of what's left in the tank. For those familiar with RP, our second attempt should be somewhere in the 8 to 9 RP range. For those unfamiliar with RP, we're looking for the presence of a sticking point, but definitely not a maximal lift. Calling the perfect third attempt is tough. It's an art and a science. It's impacted greatly by a ton of different factors. Things like your mental state, the presence of a whole bunch of hype or absence of hype, your ability to focus and concentrate, your level of experience, etc., etc., etc. We'll get more in depth on some of these sports psychology topics in a later video, but suffice to say that choosing the perfect third attempt is really what powerlifting boils down to. Squeezing that very last kilo out of yourself is kind of what this is all about. So, if you get it wrong, don't beat yourself up. Everyone gets it wrong sometimes, and it takes a hell of a lot of experience to increase that hit rate. Now, let's give some specific advice on choosing third attempts based on those scenarios we discussed earlier. First, the aggressive scenarios. Number one, if you're looking to break a record and it's your third attempt, load the record. That one's pretty straightforward. Second, if you're looking to make a qualifying total or maybe a total record, you have to weigh the probability of being able to hit this weight versus how much you might have to make up on other lifts if you miss it. Is it better to try to ek out an extra 2.5 on your squat to leave room for your bench and deadlift in case they fall short? Or is it better to go 2.5 lighter on the squat because you can probably make it up on the deadlift later? Now, there are also a few things that may change for third attempt selection based on which lift we're doing. Firstly, the bench press. Unless you're somebody who benches 200 kilos or more, chances are you don't want to be making jumps that are bigger than say 5 to 7 1/2 kilos, taking jumps of 10 kilos or more on the bench press can be really hard to execute. Often looking at the bench press score sheet after a round of third attempts can be a sea of red based on the technicality of execution, the calls and the commands. Now, when it comes to third deadlift attempt selection, we could probably make an entire video about that, and we might, but suffice to say for now, you can change your third deadlift two times. When making these changes, you can't go below the weight that's already loaded on the bar. and you have until the head referee says bar is loaded to make the change to your attempt. Sometimes managing and handling these changes in the heat of competition can trip a lot of people up. So, let's walk through a relatively simple scenario. All right, so in this scenario, there's you and your competitor Jerry. You're coming down to third deadlifts. You've put 310 kilos in for your third attempt. Jerry is attempting 297 12 kilos for his third attempt. If he makes 297, you have to pull 310 to win. However, if he misses 297, well, you could only pull 302 and still win. So, what you do is you preemptively fill out your deadlift attempt change. You put in change deadlift 302.5. Then you watch Jerry. You see if he makes the lift or not. If he makes the lift, you don't submit your change. If Jerry misses that deadlift, you're standing next to the score table ready to put that in. He gets red lights. Boom. It gets handed in. You take the minimum you need to to beat him. However, if you're not paying attention and you're not ready, Jerry goes and misses and then somebody else pulls 305 kilos. Well, you can no longer drop to 302.5 kilos. Despite that being the minimum you need to win, you'll have to pull at least 305 kilos because that's what's already loaded on the bar. Now, this is a pretty simple and straightforward example where a you're the better deadlifter, so you get to go later and just sort of watch and see what happens. Make your change relatively smooth. This scenario also assumes that you only have one person you're competing with. you're not vying for a second place finish while also trying to fend off bronze from jumping over you. However, I think this example illustrates a very simple and straightforward case of how to make changes to your third deadlift. The next concept I want to cover in this video, even though it's not directly tied to attempt selection, is going to be communication and conduct with your referees, spotters, and loaders, and with the scoring table. Firstly, many novice lifters are unsure as to why they got a call. If you have a coach or handler and they can tell you, that's going to be the easiest way to know. If you're unsure, you can either approach the jury, which is going to be a group of people seated at a table watching the meet in the same attire as the referees, or you can approach the head referee and politely ask what you got the red lights or yellow or blue for. You are also within your right to protest the call by again approaching the jury. If you're trying to protest a call, then the way to approach it is something like, "Excuse me, I believe that myself or my lifter hit depth on that. Would the jury or referees be willing to reconsider that call?" Now, it is very uncommon at the lower level for head referees or the jury to overturn calls. But if you feel you have a good handle on the rule or infraction, it's sometimes worth a shot. Just don't be that person who is approaching the head referee or jury on every single call. Not only is that going to hold up the meat, but you do that a few times and chances are you're getting waved away before you even make it to the table by the end of it. If you're approaching the bar and something is incorrectly set, whether it be the weight on the bar or the height of the rack, you can adjust the platform, generally ensuring the head referee is made aware. In the case of a misload, you'll leave the platform and the spawning loading crew will adjust it. If this happens, ensure that you get a restart on your 1 minute attempt timer. If however the rack height is wrong for you, but it is accurate to the height that you submitted when you weighed in, then you can still request the adjustment, but you do not get the timer restart. And that giant pile of information is a primer on the actual lifting process of powerlifting competition. === FILE: How to Pass All Your Powerlifting Lifts (Squat, Bench, Deadlift Rules Explained) [QpSJhj1SPbY].en.txt ===

In order to compete in powerlifting, your squat, bench press, and deadlift all need to be up to a certain standard. Your performance on the platform is going to be judged by three referees, and you have to convince at least two of those three that you've executed the lifts correctly according to the rules. In this video, we're going to take you through the specifics of lifting to competition standard in powerlifting. Welcome to episode three of the path of powerlifting series. When I did my first competition, I made a lot of mistakes. Let's take a look at my bench here. Now, in case you missed it, not only did I try to start bringing the bar down before I got the start command from the head referee, but I was also using a false grip, which is not allowed. Wait a second. Is that is that world champion and bench press world record holder Reyes Stin on my side referee there? And is that is that Ryan Stin giving me a handoff? Speaking of the Stins, they're the proprietors of Inner Strength Products and are the sponsors of this whole video series. I wanted to highlight the fact that they volunteered at and hosted my first ever powerlifting meet because I think that illustrates just how long they've been contributing to Canadian powerlifting. Yes, inner strength has great products and good prices and hella fast shipping, but the reason that we with them so hard is because they support powerlifting so hard. Inner Strength Products is for lifters and bylters and they're incredible people. I truly want to see them succeed and that's why we've decided to partner with them for the series. All those nice things being said, Rehea did still give me more than a few red lights that day. Let's get back to the video so that we can ensure that you are not going to be getting red lights at your first competition. For the sake of this video, we're going to refer to the competition standard for the lifts in the IPF. That's because the IPF is arguably the most strict of the federations. And therefore, if we use that as the reference, if your lifts pass in the IPF, then they should pass anywhere. With that being said, let's get into the rules and standards of the lifts, as well as the commands that you'll have to obey on the platform on meetday. First up, the squat. The main consideration when training your squat for competition is depth. Now, the rule book states that the crease of the hip must pass below the top of the knee joint. Squat depth is sometimes a contentious topic, but here's an illustration of the objective measure and a few camera angles showing appropriate versus missed depth. If you're training for a competition, you should ensure that you're filming yourself from various angles and make absolutely sure that you're hitting depth on every rep that you do. Beyond depth, there are still a few more considerations for the squat. You will need to receive a squat command from the head referee before beginning the descent of your squat. But bear in mind there is no up command and you do not need to pause the squat in competition. You can stand as wide or as narrow as is comfortable for you. But in order to get that squat command, there are two prerequisites. Number one, your knees need to be locked and not soft. And number two, you need to be standing erect. Now, erectness isn't strictly defined, but I've only ever seen a few people too hinged or bent forward to get a start command. As long as you don't look like this, you should be fine. The commands for the squat are squat when you're in position and you're ready to execute the rep and rack once you've stood the bar back up and locked out fully. I like to have lifters bear these things in mind when training for the squat. first taking a few seconds after unrackcking to just stand still and settle before beginning their set. And again, taking a few seconds, holding still, standing fully locked out before re-rackcking after completing the set. Up next, the bench press. Most people who train the bench press without competition in mind are just going to tap the bar to their chest and press it right back up. We call this touch and go. If you're going to start training for powerlifting, the first thing you need to do is ditch touch and go. The number one rule to transition into a powerlifting style bench press is to get comfortable pausing the bar on your chest. Now, the pause length, if I had to quantify it, is likely around.7 to 1.5 seconds long. The rule book states that the bar must be motionless on the chest, but depending on the judge or referee who's making the call, your pause may be slightly longer or shorter. When we pause, however, we have to make sure that we don't dip after the pause. If you pause the bar on your chest and then dip the bar before pressing, that's called heaving and is an infraction. You can sink the bar into your chest as much as you'd like before the pause, but you can't sink after the pause. Something else to consider is your bench grip. Now, you can grip the bar as narrow as you'd like or is as comfortable, but there is a limit to how wide you can grip on the bar. These rings in the nurling on a standard power bar are going to be 81 cm apart. The widest legal grip you can take is putting your index finger on that ring and covering it. Your head referee will be checking to ensure that even if you're max legal, you're covering the rings with your index finger. One more thing about the grip is that you must wrap your thumb around the bar. You can't use a false grip with your thumb behind the bar. Not only is this a major safety concern, but it's also necessary to fulfill the requirements in the rules of competition. There are a few more rules to consider, but luckily they're a little bit more straightforward. You must have your head down on the bench the whole time. Make sure that your head is in contact with the bench from the time you unrackck to the time that you re-rackck. The next thing to consider is your feet. When it comes to the setup and the press, the feet have to be as flat as the shoe allows and can't move from the position you set them in. The last setup rule is one that's generally agreed upon even for casual gym goers. If your butt lifts off the bench during the course of the press, that lift doesn't count. And lastly, the most contentious addition to powerlifting rules in quite some time, there is bench depth. To quote the IPF rule book, it says you must lower the underside of both elbow joints with or below the top surface of each respective shoulder joint. This rule is new and as a result the judging can be inconsistent, but what we're looking for is this part here being below this part here at the bottom of the movement. The bench press commands are the most numerous and unfortunately are also the ones I've seen the most people mess up. In the bench, once the lifter has unracked and has their elbows extended, we give a start command. And then once the bar is motionless on their chest, we have a press command. Once the bar is locked back out, much like in the squat, and the elbows are extended again, we have a rack command. Just like in the squat, when my lifters are training the bench, I always recommend they incorporate a slight pause after the unrackck and before starting the set, as well as a slight pause again after completing the set and before the re-rackck, so that we can simulate these pauses and be better prepared for midday. And finally, deadlift. When it comes to the deadlift, thankfully, things are a little bit simpler. The number one thing that I have to work with newer lifters on is ensuring that they're fully locked out and ensuring that they hold that lockout. The things that make a lockout locked out are the extension of the knees, the extension of the hips, and finally ensuring that the shoulders are in line with the rest of the torso. There's only one command in the deadlift and that command is down. This command is given only once the lifter is fully locked out. There's no start command in the deadlift and the lift is considered to have started once the lifter makes a deliberate attempt to lift the bar. That's why I always recommend a 1 to twoount hold on the lockout at the top of every deadlift in training. We also must never ever ever drop the bar in a powerlifting competition. We have to return the bar to the floor in our hands. This will have the added benefit of building more grip strength, which is certainly important in competition because there are no straps allowed in powerlifting. You'll also need to avoid ramping and hitching if you want your deadlift to pass in competition. Ramping is when you drive your knees forward under the bar to support the weight and then slowly ramp it up your thighs to lock it out. Hitching is when you jostle the bar up and down to get that little bit of momentum in order to get through a sticky lockout. One of the infractions on the deadlift is downward movement. So this up and down motion will cause your lift to be disqualified. These concepts, rules, and cues are things that we have to keep in mind at all times in powerlifting. Having a supportive and encouraging community to remind you about these things as well as worldclass coaches analyzing your technique in video reviews weekly in check-ins as well as a massive library of programs. That's what's on offer with the Calgary Barbell app. You can check it out. The link is in the description box below. If you can get these things locked in, you're going to be absolutely ready to lift come time for your first competition. In the next episode of our path of powerlifting series, we're going to cover anything you might need to pack to bring to a powerlifting meet. We'll see you there.

We're reducing stimulus in general about one hour before we go to bed. And we're trying to stick to a sleep schedule, rising and falling asleep around the same times of day every day of the week. If you're training for a powerlifting meet, then you're an athlete. able to cheat by doping now i think it's also really worth mentioning that just because you sign up for ipf affiliated federations membership card doesn't mean somebody's gonna come knocking at your door and demanding you pee in a cup this really only happens for a certain top percentile in the sport who are competitive either internationally or nationally depending on the national federation there are also a few tiers of monitoring now number one there's what's called the registered testing pool which basically means that you've just given your information ahead of time so they have you in the database and chances are they're a little bit more likely to test you in a competition the second tier to this program which is where myself and a lot of other lifters you might follow on And now, feet up bench. The feet up bench press is a great exercise if you're somebody who finds themselves wobbling around on the bench. If you struggle with keeping your shoulder blades tight throughout maybe a higher rep sets and then that translates over into your 1RM. Well, the feet up bench takes the legs and the feet completely out of the equation, which forces the upper body to have to do all of the stabilizing work itself. It also in some ways acts as a pseudo deficit bench where there's maybe slightly more range of motion because you're not able to use your feet to drive your chest up as much. You're going to end up with tiny little bit more range of motion. For that reason, I really like it as a hypertrophy exercise. Uh something to be utilized with less specific protocols, maybe higher rep ranges, but I also think this can be a great way to build that strength into the stability, right? Kind of pairing those two things, synergy and getting the best of both worlds. I probably wouldn't be doing like heavy singles and triples here, but I do think you could probably push sets of four to six and get some good results out of it. As a little tip for when you're doing the feet up bench press, here's how I recommend the setup be. Right, you're going to go through your entire bench setup with your feet down on the ground like you normally would, as if you're doing a normal competition bench press. Set everything up. Go through to the point where you unrackck, put your butt down, and make putting your feet up the very last thing that you do. That way, you give yourself the best odds of maintaining the best position that you can.

=== FILE: If You Miss Benches Off the Chest, You Need This [7kFLTYFdxZM].en.txt ===

Next up, let's talk about the pin press. So, let's talk a little bit about the pin press. If you're somebody who's issue in the bench press comes when you initiate the press out of the paws, well, pin press might just be the perfect accessory for you. The way to set it up is to try to get the pins to take the weight just as the bar touches the chest. If you don't have a rack with really nice close pole spacing like this one here, you may end up in a situation where you can choose either a little bit above the chest or a little bit below where you usually touch and have to sink to touch. If that comes up, I recommend you go for the higher of the two settings. If you have to sink, you're going to lose a bunch of position during the pause and it's going to kind of defeat the purpose of the movement. When you're executing this movement, always start from the top and unrackck as normal. I don't see a good reason to do pin presses starting from the bottom. The rep will consist of bringing the bar down at the speed that you normally bring the bar down. You may need to have a little bit of extra control at the bottom because we don't want the bar to fall on the pins and we don't want the bar to bounce off of the pins. We want to be able to unload maybe 70 or 80% of the weight onto the pins without completely relaxing and then press having to break inertia off of the pins. Just a quick note, you can use some variations of this that perhaps focus a little bit more on different parts of the range of motion, but the most universal variation of the pin press I can recommend is doing it at chest height. === FILE: Linear Progression Won’t Last Forever - Here’s What’s Next [U2NUkpL-uZU].en.txt ===

The second model of progression we're going to look at here is a wave progression or undulating progression. After a while, linear progression is not going to work anymore. Once you're of runway on your linear progression, you want to start planning some fluctuation into your training. Usually, this looks like a period of time where you intentionally decrease volume while increasing intensity, hit a little reset, and then repeat that process again. If you look at most of the 50 plus expertly designed programs in the Calgary barbell app, that's their general structure. The basic idea behind this progression structure is that you build up, back off, and then repeat. By manipulating the variables of rep ranges, the intensity, maybe even the number of sets, you'll move from adding weight each week to now adding weight each block. So, you'll be able to prolong that progression as you get more experienced.

=== FILE: Longevity： How To Thrive In Powerlifting [JK_svFaeyDk].en.txt ===

hello everybody today I want to talk about longevity and the sport of power lifting now this is something that I get asked about pretty routinely and to give a bit of a disclaimer maybe I'm not the perfect model of this I've only been competing in powerlifting for seven years which the grand scheme of things might not be that long and especially compared to some lifters that have been around unfortunately will end up deterring a lot of younger lifters now there are a few main points that I want to talk about today one of those is gonna be being more process-oriented and this kind of runs parallel with intrinsic motivation we'll go through the differences between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation and how that can contribute to your success long-term and the last thing I want to talk about is focusing on your locus of control all these things kind of tie in together pretty well so I'll try to make this nice and succinct and tie everything in together as we get to the end of it all so the first thing we're gonna dive into is sort of defining some of these terms now the first big comparison we want to make to illustrate for you guys is gonna be the difference between being goal oriented which is very much running parallel to being extrinsic ly motivated versus being process oriented or you know very commonly known as being a little bit more intrinsically motivated now goal orientation or extrinsic motivation is going to be linking your sort of feelings of success and feelings of self-worth even to exterior motivators and exterior factors so things like winning awards beating competitors placing on the podium breaking records hitting qualifying totals and all that kind of stuff now while extrinsic motivation I think is important when we're talking about acting our efforts if we don't have something like that to work towards it can feel hard to get motivated in the first place however what I think more people could use more of is more intrinsic motivation focusing on the process trying to set yourself up for little wins and training and this is a big one so if the weight on the bar didn't go up this week did you move the bar better was the RPE a little bit less did you maybe lock out your deadlift it's better was your squat depth better did you pause your bench for a more clean rep setting yourself up for these feelings of success even perceived feelings of success can be a big step towards harnessing and cultivating more intrinsic motivation so when we're talking about process orientation we're talking about learning to essentially fall in love with the process of training to learn to enjoy the day-to-day and the act of going in and improving however slightly on some quality of your training so that when you get injured or you plateau and things that were extrinsically motivated by like those qualifying totals those medals those records aren't getting any closer at least we can focus on how much we enjoy doing things every single time we come into the gym and improving on those like I said however slight the quality is and making those little improvements from day to day and from session to session so my point here is that by shift in the torso which shifts the weight which is an energy leak which means that you're not performing as efficiently as possible because things are shifting and changing in your trunk as you go through the lift so I would say try to recreate that position you're in on the way up on the way down so that you're consistently locked in through the trunk and consistent in torso position as opposed to having that shift in that moment of change in the bottom which is that that's what's gonna throw you off if anything and I think that's it for today guys and gals so I want to thank everybody for joining along with us here today hopefully everybody got something out of it and enjoyed listening to my sweet soothing tones talk you through some some some power lifting again if you guys are interested in submission the email is form check Friday at gmail.com and yeah stay tuned for a lot more great content and thanks for watching we'll see you guys in the next video

=== FILE: My FAVOURITE Bench Press Cue (Try this if your bench is struggling) [oZ8r_gokCoY].en.txt ===

what's up guys we're here today is to talk about my favorite tip or queue in the bench press now the biggest reason that I like this queue so much is that it incorporates a number of different components of the lift and it forces the lifter to perform four separate things at once all encompassed under this one queue of reaching your chest up to the bar the first thing that we're going to talk about is it helps the lifter create an arch now why the hell is an arch important first off its gonna put the shoulder blades in a good position it's gonna trim the range of motion a little bit and it's gonna put you in a decline or a kind of decline where you're gonna create a biomechanical advantage the second thing that it's gonna do is it's gonna reduce the range of motion even more so than probably your standard arch if you're actively reaching your chest up you're reinforcing that arch you're reaching higher you're trimming that range of motion even just another extra half inch and in the bottom position of the benchpress that can go a long ways the third thing that helps us do is to create and maintain a good amount of leg drive now I see a lot of lifters come down and sink into the chest with loose legs and then try to use leg drive to kick-start the bar off the chest now in my general experience this leads to a lot of inconsistencies this leads to the butt coming up off the bench this leads to different positions from wrap to wrap it's just a number of things that can go wrong when you bench like this by reaching the chest up to the bar we're driving through the heels the glutes are squeezed the bus on the bench and everything is tight throughout the whole range of motion there's no stop gap in the force production or in the stability of your body on the bench and the fourth and final thing that this cue is gonna help you do is gonna help you keep from dumping the bar now when we come down a lot of times it's a simple matter if there's too much range of motion for the shoulder to go through in a good position so lifters end up dumping the bar shoulders roll forward out of position now you'll notice a lot of these cues kind of run into each other but I've separated them this way to try to make my point better like I said if we can get the lifter to trim that range of motion we're gonna be able to get a nice light touch keeping the bar in control keep tension into the bar keeping the weight of the bar in the hands and not dumping onto the chest in the bottom position of the bench press now I will say sort of one caveat here and that is that you need to maintain this queue throughout the lift if we come off the chest and stop reaching up and fall back into the bench I mean maybe that can be beneficial on a 1 rep max you're in competition where you're just doing whatever the hell you can to get that one rep but if you do that on a set of reps you're gonna have a significant drop-off in the amount of power you're able to put from rep 1 to rap 2 by losing so much position anyways guys I hope that's something that you can all incorporate into your lifting and find some advantage with and are able to get a little bit more to your bench press just by doing that one cue of reaching your chest up to the bar thanks very for tuning in and if you want to see more videos like this just let us know in the comments below leave a like if you liked it hit that subscribe button and we will see you guys next time bye bye

=== FILE: Neutral Grip Bench Press #powerlifting #benchpress [1OUVbbdNBPo].en.txt ===

All right, this is a neutral grip bar or a football bar or I believe a arch nemesis bar if you're bells of steel. You might be looking at this thing like why the hell would anybody ever use that? One of the best utilities I found for this is as a tool to work around janky shoulders in the bench. I got a number of lifters who I've coached over the years who get into situations where they have prolonged pain symptoms in their shoulders and can't straight bar press or can't do it very comfortably or can't use the full range of motion. So something like this allowing that shoulder to be at a at a fairly different angle and still train the bench can be really really useful. I've also had lifters use a reverse grip bench and just take a straight bar upside down. It's super weird. If you're going to try it, make sure you have a spotter and a handoff because it is awkward as hell. But this is a pretty good way to get around it. I've been using it recently because my shoulder is a little janky at the moment. It seems to be a good way to get some pressing stress and stimulus on there. Gives a good tricep pump if you're using one of the inside handles. And this one actually detaches. You can strap it onto a cable, pull on it if you want, do some lat pull downs or rows or whatever. And there are more robust versions of it if you want to get into something that you're going to do a little more heavy pressing on. Check it out if you have access to one. Try it out.

welcome back to Calgary barbell guys today we are going to talk a little bit about the pin squat now if you don't know the pin squat is going to be executed similar to a competition squat except at the bottom of your squat the bar is actually going to come to rest on the safety pins um this is going to deload the bar completely and you're going to have to restart from a dead stop and break inertia with that bar before you can finish the lift so some of the reasons you might want to use this lift are to de velop strength out of the bottom it can be very it can be used very similarly to a pause squat but one of the differences that I see between this and a pause squat is with a pause squat you can kind of loosen up and you can rely on a little bit of stretch reflex but with a pin squat if you go any further below your bottom position uh or loosen it all you're going to have a really really hard time breaking it off the pins because that bar is at a dead stop it's not coming with you to that lower Point um some of the mistakes we often see in the pin squat are going to be either setting the bar or the pins the safety pins too high or too low uh and that's going to sort of mess up the groove of the lift and change things a little bit we also sometimes see people start from the bottom now this is something that I don't Advocate uh with either a pin bench press or the pin squat going to be able to lock the back in we're going to be able to put anything everything into uh as a sort of a better position for a lack of better words another mistake we often see is people === FILE: Pause Deadlifts： The Most Underrated Accessory？ [MbLa3-woKxw].en.txt ===

Number four, one of my personal favorites, the pause deadlift. These are incredibly effective at teaching positional awareness and control, especially if you tend to rush your pull or if you have troubles with the start of the lift or start position. So, I typically recommend these are done two different ways. One for sumo, one for conventional. In the sumo deadlift, we want to pause within an inch of breaking the bar off the floor. very very bottom end of the range of motion. That's because generally in sumo, this is either where we lose position or it's the toughest part of the lift. For conventional, however, I generally recommend lifters pause a little higher, usually just below the knee because that's where lifters struggle again with that transition between the push at the start of the pull and the pull at the end of the deadlift. Right.

=== FILE: Pause Deadlifts： You’re Probably Doing Them Wrong [pLU7ftEKB1E].en.txt ===

Couple practical tips for the pause deadlift. Number one, it should feel like a push off the floor and it should feel like a push out of the pause. We want to feel like in this movement we're starting the lift twice. It's going to emphasize that bottom position. It's going to get you stronger off the floor. Another tip, pause it. Don't just start slow. Don't just like hiccup during the movement. Pause it. Hold it for a solid two count and then finish the movement. If you have to put a caption on it for somebody to recognize that you paused it, you didn't pause it. Lastly, don't take advantage of position during the pause. I see a lot of sumo lifters in particular lift the bar off the floor, then during their pause, they'll wedge their hips in harder and get more upright. So coming out of the pause, they're in a totally different position, and they're actually then advantaged out of that position. No. No. We want you to pause in the position you're going to be in. Come out of the position you're going to be in. We want this to be transferable to your competition deadlift.

=== FILE: Pause Squats vs.Pin Squats (Which should you do？) [Rz0OsNxZwys].en.txt ===

in powerlifting training there are ton of popular variations to exercises and a lot of people will claim that this one is the best or that one is the best in my opinion the best ones are gonna be the ones that are most specific that is most like the competition lifts that they're meant to enhance so today we're gonna talk a little bit about pause squats and pin squats what are the differences the main mistakes in execution and the reasons that you might use one over the other why use exercise variation at all in your powerlifting programming I think there are a number of reasons that make exercise variation a useful tool in programming for powerlifting number one it allows the lifter to create some technical proficiency become better at positional awareness and target certain ranges of motion in terms of feeling where they are in the lift and feeling and understanding what they're doing and how to move the other thing is it's a tool for coaches and lifters to problem-solve certain ranges of motion certain joint angles where lifters might not perform optimally or might be weak as well it's worth mentioning that exercise variation can reduce monotony by providing a novel stimulus in your training which can be helpful from a psychological standpoint first let's talk about the pause squat now one of the benefits of the pause squat that sets it somewhat apart from the pinspot is that it requires no extra equipment whatever bar you have kicking around whatever rack you'd normally squat out of will be fine for this the execution of the pause squat is as such all you're gonna do is you're going to use an isometric contraction in the bottom position of your squat to stop the position pause and deaden the stretch reflex and then come back up as normal this deadening of the stretch reflex and focus on the lifter creating that bottom position and holding it will increase proprioception in the bottom by practicing the skill of maintaining good positioning as well as strengthen the lifter in those specific joint angles produced at the bottom of the range of motion if a lifter is someone who finds themselves often missing at the bottom of the squat and by missing I mean failing a rep or finds themselves rocking too far forward in the bottom of their squat or thirdly is somebody who bottoms out and often goes too deep more deep than necessary in their squat the pause squat can be a very useful variation there are a couple of common mistakes that I often see in the execution of the pod squad the first of those mistakes is going to lift their bottoms out or relies on a loose bottom position as opposed to creating a nice tight isometric contraction in the bottom position like so as opposed to coming down into a nice tight controlled position bracing and holding and then coming back up the other mistake I see a lot of people make is very short quick pauses now when you're in the bottom position of a squat especially with any appreciable amount of weight on your back it can be tempting to count very quickly having a friend or training partner count for you should help allow you to make sure that you are taking enough time in the bottom to actually dead in the stretch reflex and to create a good isometric contraction for the strengthening stimulus in the bottom position a lot of people will pause very quickly as opposed to coming down one one thousand two one thousand and using a much more appropriate isometric one of the things that I think differentiates the pause spot from the pin squat is that the pause squat forces the lifter to create the bottom position without relying on any sort of external cue to tell them what position to be in or where to stop their depths at the bottom next up the pin squat now the pin squat is going to require some equipment you're gonna need a rack with adjustable safety heights so you can set the pins at an appropriate depth to unload the bar slightly as you reach the bottom of your squat now the only other way you can do this without Iraq that has adjustable safety pins is to put some sort of spotting blocks or boxes on the outsides to take the weight off the plates a little bit as you reach the bottom the execution of the pin squat is going to be as such basically all you're gonna do is squat as normal once you reach the bottom the way it's gonna unload slightly to the pins and then you stand it back up if you're a lifter who suffers from strength issues in the bottom position of your squat and more specifically if technique issues in terms of running into the squat morning issues with your bar position the pin squat can be a great variation to use to try to fix those the issues or common mistakes that I see in the pin squat are as follows the two biggest ones are gonna be unloading too much onto the pins which as you can tell really disconnect from the bar and you're gonna have a really hard time maintaining any sort of positioning again sort of defeating the purpose and falling into the trap of committing the technical error we're trying to fix the other one is gonna be not unloading enough so essentially just pause squatting above the pins barely making contact and coming back up basically we want to try to find a sweet spot between unloading too much and not unloading enough onto the pins the way that I advocate lifters do this is to try to make sure that the bar comes to a complete stop on the pins but that you're not losing that feeling of engagement and connection to the bar another thing that's worth saying about pin squats is I don't recommend starting them from the bottom now the reason for this is that starting them from the bottom is going to make it almost impossible to create a good tight squat position this in turn is gonna lessen the load that you're gonna be able to use which subsequently will lessen the specificity and the transferability which is a long-winded way of starting from the bottom is gonna make you do them light which is gonna limit how much they'll actually carry over to your competition spot so the biggest difference is in the two movements as you can see is obviously in the execution but another thing to take into consideration is the necessity for different equipment now you can do a pause squat anywhere you choose whereas you need a power rack with appropriate settings for pin Heights in order to do a pin squat both of these exercises variations would be appropriate for a lifter who consistently you lose his position in the bottom range of motion of their squat or is weak out of the bottom of their squat there are a few subtle differences and how and why I would prescribe them if you find yourself or your athlete that you're coaching maybe is a lifter who has a tendency to rock forward too far in the bottom is consistently losing their position onto their toes and having balance issues in the bottom of their squat as well as perhaps squatting too deep I believe that is a strong case for the use of positive spots specifically conversely if the lifter specifically has issues with the bar position on their back like the bar rolling their up their back rounding or the very classic sort of squat morning pattern where the hips rise up behind the lifter I would say that's more a case for the use of the pin squat now I make this distinction based specifically on that === FILE: Pause Squats： Brutal But Effective #powerlifting #squat [jGFB5yxhd5E].en.txt ===

I've got a pretty good squat, but I want more. The first accessory movement that I'm going to talk about is the paused squat. Now, it's a pretty basic one. All you're going to do is a squat and pause in the bottom. But there is some nuance to it. The pause squat is going to be a really good tool for helping you build positioning in the bottom and for helping you build strength coming out of the bottom. When we pause at that joint angle that we're hitting in the hole, we're going to strengthen that joint angle. We're going to get better at breaking inertia and changing directions on the bar. One of my biggest pieces of advice for the pause squat is to make sure that you're not falling into the bottom. We don't want to be relaxed when we get to the bottom of a pause squat. Depth is not necessarily the main concern of a paused squat. Chances are your pause squats are going to be just on the line if you're doing them well. Because in a competition squat, we're going to use that little bit of looseness to bounce just a bit and get that extra little bit of depth. In a pause squat, you're pumping the brakes. You're putting the brakes on on the way down to make sure that we are holding a really, really tight and well braced bottom position. We also want to avoid bouncing out of the bottom before we come up. A lot of lifters will pause and then dip and come up. That's going to make you coming out of the pause way easier and kind of defeats the purpose of the movement. So, if you're struggling with the consistency in your bottom position or maybe you're starting to panic as you get down there, the pause squat can be a great tool to work on those things as well as just building a lot of strength in the bottom.

=== FILE: Progress Isn't Just Adding Weight - Here's How [WMGLolTq004].en.txt ===

So, it turns out Kel Supre that there are other ways to progress beyond just adding weight to the bar. And the first of those ways is to add or remove sets or reps. Let's say you're running a 3x5, right? That's your progression. 3x5, you smacking weight on there every week or every time you squat. Who knows? How can you progress that once you come up against it? Well, you could do a 3x six and and try to keep the weight the same. You could do a 3x4 in order to add more weight without failing or overshooting. Or you could do a 4x5. You could add or remove sets of reps to make it more reasonable to progress for longer. You can also try implementing accessory movements. If you're stalling out on the big three squat bench press deadlift, try out some variations of those movements. You can check out the video that we just did recently on my top five deadlift accessories. I think probably in the description below or maybe on the screen somewhere here. You can also work on trying to improve your bar speed. Maybe you track this meticulously and you have a velocity tracking device of some kind. Maybe you don't. But progressing bar speed is not only something that you can probably measure visually if you make a decent enough jump in how fast you're able to move a weight, but also it can be a good goal when it comes to getting stuck progressing the weight itself.

Point number three, think big picture. A lot of the times when we get to the sort of bleeding edge of progress, whatever that might be for you, we need to start zooming out a little bit. When you're a novice lifter and you can just do 3x5 for 4 months and put 20 kilos on all your lifts, that's pretty cool. you squat on Monday and then you squat on Wednesday and your squat gets better and then you squat on Friday and your squat gets better. That's not the case with advanced lifters. That's why it's important that we zoom out. And while things might look a little convoluted or seem a bit illogical in the short term, we have to think about the contributions to long-term progress, cuz that's what we're talking about when we're getting into the higher ends of strength development. A good phrase that I've I've heard mostly from Taylor at Calgary Barbell is to think in months and years, not days and weeks. === FILE: Push Your Accessory Work #powerlifting [Yj-_biCISWw].en.txt ===

If I had to give you one piece of lifting advice, knowing nothing about you, nothing about your training, nothing about your goals, just knowing that you're some kind of power lifter, you do the squat, bench, and deadlift, and you do some accessory movements, here's what I would say. I would tell you that you probably need to go a little lighter on your competition work on your squat bench and deadlift and you probably need to go a little heavier on your accessories on your leg presses, your split squats, your rows, and that kind of stuff because so much of our progress on SPD movements is skill-based. And because it demands so much more from the system when it comes to recovery, it's really easy to overdo those things. We also get really tied up in the numbers. We get our egos involved and we want more weight on the bar with those. When it comes to the accessories, we can recover fast. We're usually locked in maybe on some kind of machine or something and can push really hard with minimal impact to our other lift. I've given this little piece of advice to a few clients, some friends, some family, and it's already drastically improved their training. So maybe carry that philosophy into a few sessions and see how it goes.

=== FILE: RDL vs. Stiff-Leg Deadlift – What’s the Difference？ [TjpPM0obe9Y].en.txt ===

Okay, so the first thing I want to do here is differentiate the Romanian deadlift from the stiff-legged deadlift. A Romanian deadlift is going to start from the top. It starts with the eccentric or lowering phase. You're going to go down just past the knees and come back up. That's one rep. Picking the bar up doesn't count as a rep. A stiff leg deadlift, you're going to start from a dead stop every time. You're going to go all the way to the floor. You're going to keep your hips much, much higher with less knee bend. This is your start position for a stiff leg. When you're doing a Romanian deadlift, you want to try to find a good balance between pressure on your heels. So, we can feel a lot of good hamstring stretch and tension and allowing the knees to come forwards enough that by the time the bar gets to the bottom, we are getting a little bit of that quad feeling and a little bit of that push to start the lift. That way, it's going to carry over better into your deadlift and help with that transition in the competition lift itself.

=== FILE: RPE Misconception 2 #powerlifting [6Dv6m5BjQiQ].en.txt ===

RP is just there to let coaches be lazy. Write a number in like a man. This one couldn't be further from the truth. I'd argue that putting a percentage that your lifter has to hit no matter what into a spreadsheet is far more lazy. Using RP well as a coach means that you're taking the time to educate and contextualize the use of RP with your athlete. You're teaching them what an RP8 means to you, what you expect to see when an RP8 is written, and then they're having to do the work on their end to put the right weight on the bar and execute to a standard. All of this information is contained within me saying RP8 to an athlete, but all the subtext and the context and the nuance and circumstance of that RP8 are all things that need to be built up over the course of developing a relationship with the athlete. So RP is really a a linguistic tool. It's a way of quantifying and communicating more effectively with your athlete while teaching them that they have to be more independent and they have to do a better job in order to meet your expectations. Or you could write 200 kilos because you think that's what they have to

=== FILE: RPE Misconception 3 #powerlifting [diworonwDvY].en.txt ===

RP lets lifters be lazy. I think most of the time when people misinterpret RP, they they tend to put too much weight on the bar. If you're going to go through all the trouble of of getting a coach and trying to understand RP and putting in all this work to be better at training for strength, you're not then going to go into the gym and think, hm, how do I do less and work less hard? Sure, people underestimate their RPS. It happens. But I really don't think it's this systemic or or integral problem with using RP that everyone is going to be a wuss.

=== FILE: RPE and RIR Are Basically the Same #powerlifting [7tmJ15Q1Juc].en.txt ===

Well, actually, if the only thing you're using to rate your RP is how many reps left in the tank, you're using RIIR or reps in reserve. My hot take here is that for 99.9999% of people, it doesn't matter. They are similar enough that for all of our intents and purposes, reps left in the tank, RP, it's all the same. The formula is 10 minus how many reps more you could have

=== FILE: STOP Benching With Straight Wrists! [i-QZYFsCv9E].en.txt ===

Are you trying to bench press with straight wrists? Stop it. You may actually be sabotaging your bench and leaving kilos on the bar by trying to bench like you're throwing a punch. But stacked joints are good in powerlifting, right? Look at the squat, look at the deadlift, and even in the bench press, right? Well, yes and no. In the case of the bench, it's way more important that the weight is stacked over the wrist than it is that your wrist is straight. And I see way too many lifters mess this up. So, what's the solution? How should we be pressing? Well, you should be pressing with your wrist bent slightly backwards and the bar low in your palm. === FILE: STOP Losing Position in the Deadlift - Fix This NOW [HArc-gyOrgI].txt ===

 Hello and welcome back to Calgary Barbell. I'm Bryce and I want to help you fix your deadlift. Is this you? Do your hips shoot up into the air as soon as you start your deadlift? If so, this is leaving you in a poor position to get the most out of your deadlift. You are being inefficient in this position and you're missing out on valuable stimulus for both strength and hypertrophy and I don't want that for you. I want you to get strong and jacked. So let's talk about how we fix this issue. Reason number one, rushing the start of the deadlift. In order to help explain this, I like to break the deadlift down a little bit. In the deadlift, what happens when we lose our position and the hips fly up is we're not being patient in the first pull. The reason this is important is because if we allow that first pull to be a little heavier, to feel a little heavier, I should say, and to be a little bit slower, that's going to allow us to stay in a better position for the rest of the pull. A lot of times when we have people whose hips shoot up, they get out of position off the floor, they struggle with lock up. They either lose a bunch of back position, or they just have way too much range of motion through the hips to get to lock up. So by learning to be a little bit patient through that first pull, letting it be a little slower, we're going to end up allowing ourselves to preserve that more upright position for the second pull for the rest of the lift. Reason number two, inefficient position at the start of the deadlift. The second issue and concept that I want to illustrate here is the idea of your hips rising because you've chosen and are starting from an inefficient position. A lot of the times when we see hips rise in the deadlift, it's because we've set them too low to start off with. In some instances, the hips rising is us making up for that and putting our hips into a better position. However, because of the fact that we're not setting them intentionally, a lot of times this will mean that the hip height and angle that we end up pulling from is going to vary quite a bit from rep to rep and will continue to get higher throughout a set. If we can find an ideal start position and start with our hips in that position at that height, realistically, we're going to be able to be much more consistent. And anytime we can increase the consistency of our lifts, we are doing good things. I think a lot of more novice lifters, especially in the sumo deadlift, tend to think that lower hips is wrote better. That is always better when in actuality, I think there is such a thing and this applies to conventional as well as setting your hips too low. If we can be conscious instead of thinking of hip height, whether our hips are higher or low, if we can think about just finding the tension, that should guide us to a place where we end up with the right hip height. So what I mean by that is incorporating a process within your setup where you're thinking about good, even foot pressure. You've got good pressure through the ball of your foot and your heels. You're finding tension through the hips and hamstrings as you pull yourself into position. You're finding that adequate kind of balancing resistance from your quads, right? You're pushing against the bar as you pull into position. And finally, we're also finding tension through the trunk, the mid and upper back, finding good lat tension in order to brace our torso for the pull. So if we can incorporate all of those ways of finding tension and find that spot where we have good balance and full body tension, we don't have to worry about bringing our hips up or sitting our hips down because once we've found that tension, we'll have found the ideal start position for your limb length. Now, maybe you're not exactly sure which of these faults apply to you. Maybe you're struggling more with your squat or your bench press. Let's get back to the video. Reason number three, not understanding how to push when you pull. The third concept here that's going to help you fix your deadlift is knowing how to push when you pull. Now it sounds weird because we constantly talk about the deadlift as a pull. We say we're going to do deadlifts today, we're going to do pulls today. What are you doing? Well, I'm doing some pulls. We're pulling. But if you can understand that that first phase of the movement is a push, you're going to be in a much better place to hold your position off the floor. You need to learn to be comfortable being slightly over the bar. And again, this kind of goes hand in hand with people who sit their hips down too far. If we can allow ourselves to be a little bit further over the bar in terms of how our shoulder blade lines up with the bar, we're going to be able to better find that feeling of leg pressing. When we start the deadlift, I want you to think about pushing the floor away as opposed to pulling on the bar. Many lifters make the mistake of trying to pull back on the bar as they're starting the lift. And what this does is it forces them to work against themselves. Either the hips will go up behind you and you're just negating everything you're trying to do. Or if you manage to somehow start a lift in that position, your knees are going to push the bar away and probably your hips are going to shoot up behind you and you're going to be out of position. It seems counterintuitive, but sometimes being slightly further over the bar will allow you to line things up in a better way so that you can maintain that tension in your hips as you start the lift and find that feeling of leg pressing. Push the floor away, push the earth away for that matter. And then you're going to have a better start position. You're going to be able to maintain the hip height as you start the lift by pushing when you pull. Reason number four, poor bracing. Concept number four is going to be working to find and maintain the right brace. In some instances, people's hips will rise because they're unable to find and use that connection between the shoulders and the lats and the upper body, ribcage and up into the hips and knees. If there's a disconnect in this area, a lot of the times we won't be able to hold position and then those hips come up. What we need to do here is try to tie those areas together. When I cue a lifter in the deadlift, a lot of times what I'll get them to think about is trying to pull down on the bar, row it or roll it into themselves to point their elbows towards the back of the room. A little bit of external rotation in some instances helps. The big thing here with finding the brace and one of the other faults that I think a lot of people make is they tend to pull the shoulder blades back. People will pull into retraction instead of making their arms long and trying to pull the shoulder blade down into depression. When we pull properly into depression, we should feel mostly some lat contraction and that's going to be a huge cornerstone in making sure that we're able to build and maintain our brace in the start position. Another concept that I think people struggle with is that bracing in the deadlift and pulling into extension are not always the same thing. A lot of people will look at a deadlift where the lifter's back rounds even a little bit and think, oh my god that's dangerous and that's wrong. When in actuality that's probably a very optimal brace for that person. A lot of lifters also will pull into extension and think that by arching their back they're creating the best brace, they're creating the strongest position and the least likelihood of them going into too much extension and losing the force transfer. So I want to make it clear that extension is not the same as a strong brace. However, some lifters will brace in a bit of extension and the biggest indicator of whether or not you've found this optimal brace, whether it be more flexed or more extended, is going to be whether or not your back position changes as the bar comes off the floor. If as the bar leaves the floor we're able to maintain our brace and our positioning in terms of how flexed or extended we are, we're probably in a good back position. If we're super, super extended and as the bar leaves the floor we lose a bunch of that extension, we're probably overextending. So think about that, record your lift from the side and see whether or not you're going through a huge amount of change in your brace as you pick the bar. === FILE: Slow Down. Get Stronger. #powerlifting #squats [8-jLU-AdFZg].en.txt ===

The third exercise that we're talking about today is the tempo squat. Now, you could use a number of different tempos in the tempo squat. Tempo just being the speed with which you're executing the movement. Now, quick primer on tempos. There are usually three numbers in the description of a tempo. It's formatted as number- dash number. The first number is always the eentric or lowering phase of the movement. The second number is always an isometric or a pause or lack thereof denoted by a zero. The final number is always the concentric or upwards phase of the movement. And again, if this is just done at normal speed, there's a zero. So, all that is to say, generally when I get to tempo squats, what I'm recommending is something like a 300 tempo squat. So, we're taking extra care and extra consideration and extra time on the descent of the movement. The reason this is useful is because it helps lifters figure out positions. We're not just speeding through the positions. We're not just again falling into the bottom. We're instead creating a purposeful series of movements that can be really effective as a learning tool. I think most lifters in terms of just learning the positions, getting a little bit more time under tension 30 0 or even incorporating a tempo paused squat mish mashing the two together with a 320 3ount eccentric 2count pause normal on the way up can be a great way to go about it. But the basic idea here is that you're just you're just slowing it down. You're slowing it down on the way down. A really important tip for the tempo squat is to keep the tempo even. If it's a 30 0 tempo squat, don't go one 2 3 and fall through the last half of the range of motion. You know what? Most common mistake people will slow through the first part and then just kind of bail on the tempo and do a normal squat. We want to try to smooth out the tempo. So, it's a three count. One, two, three, up. Right? It's not one 2 3. That's just cutting out half the tempo. And arguably the most important part of the tempo is that last little bit before the bottom, because that's the part that people mess up.

=== FILE: Squat Stuck？ This Is Probably Why [IdVdS54H8js].en.txt ===

If your squat is stuck, feeling off, or is just uncomfortable, chances are you're making one of these five mistakes. I see these in intermediate, novice, all the way up to advanced lifters. And fixing these mistakes can help you on your path to building a big old squat. Mistake number one, incorrect bracing. The most common and fundamental issue that I see with lifters squats is their brace. Bracing is about more than just taking a big breath in before you squat. A lot of lifters mess this up by flaring the ribs way out and kicking their hips too far behind them, creating a whole bunch of extension on the descent of the squat. Now, this is an issue because you're going to have problems with getting to depth comfortably, or maybe you'll see a really pronounced sticking point as a result of it. In order to fix your bracing, what you want to be doing is contracting your abs super duper hard, clamping your ribs down on top of your abs, and trying to keep your hips tucked in, keeping your pelvis stacked with the rest of your back as you descend in the squat. Ideally, you want to maintain this position throughout the whole of the squat, which requires that you learn how to hinge and understand how to hinge. If you want more information on this bracing topic specifically, there's a couple videos we'll link in the description.

=== FILE: Stop Popping Forward in the Squat (Fix This Common Mistake) [DlMX44UqXeY].en.txt ===

All right, welcome back to Calgary Barbell. Today we are going to work on the number one issue I see with novice and intermediate squats that isn't bracing. Well, the issue is the pop or slide forward in the bottom of your squat. So, a lot of lifters when they squat are doing a really good job of the squat till about here. Then what happens is we loosen up and everything pops forwards. The knees pop forwards. In a lot of cases, the heels will even come up and we lose all the tension in the posterior chain. So again, we're good to about here and then we just kind of loosen and dip. You can see my heel come up there. My depth probably doesn't look very good. And there are a number of reasons that this is a problem. So like I said, the heel comes up. We're losing balance. All of our weight is shifting forward. we're getting pretty far away from our center of mass, center of gravity, and it's going to mask your depth, right? So, we think about if my elbow is the heel and this is the knee, the further forward it goes, the lower it goes vertically, right? If the knee stays back a little bit, it sits higher. Why is this important? Because in order to get powerlifting depth, we need the crease of the hip to go below the top of the knee. If the top of the knee is moving down as the crease of the hip moves down, makes it way harder to get depth. That's thing number one. Don't make type one errors. Don't miss depth. The next thing, when we pop forward like that, like I said, we're losing all of the tension in the posterior chain, right? We're losing all of the the stability and the tightness in the hips and hamstrings. Now, what happens because of that? Again, let's demonstrate. So when we have this pop forwards, what usually follows is us having to refind tension. So we're good to here. We pop forwards and then we get this really quick shot out of the bottom. We end up being pitched forward. The bar is way in front of my center foot and I'm trying to refind that posterior chain tension, usually resulting in a sticking point in the bar rolling up the back in us getting pulled further forwards. Right. and then we're grinding out the rest of the squat. All right, so there are a ton of reasons we might want to fix this issue. How do we fix it? One thing that helped me that's super easy to do was just switching flats. When squatting in flats, I found it way more easy to tell when I was popping forwards when I ended up losing that position on my feet because I can feel where the weight is distributed on my feet a lot better. The most straightforward and direct way to address this is to simply work on how you're descending through that bottom third of the range of motion. So instead of going loose, a lot of times I think people do this and loosen up because they're afraid of getting further pitched forward. They're afraid of leaning the right amount in terms of their torso angle. So they loosen up to avoid leaning so they can pop forward. the hips and knees and everything shoot forward, but they stay upright, which doesn't end up helping us. The biggest way that I like to cue this for lifters that I coach and work with through the wonderful Calgary barbell app that you can check out in the description link below is to kind of slow things down and to just think about reaching back in the bottom of the squat. Right? So, like I said, most lifters are good to about here. From this point, a lot of lifters instinct is just to loosen up. What we want to do is start reaching back in the hips to try to keep the feet flat and maintaining our trunk angle, our torso angle. Right? So staying back, keeping those hips back, keeping things center of foot, maintaining good pressure through the front and back of the foot. Another reason people mess this up is because they're trying to overcorrect for this specific issue. In a lot of cases, lifters know they pop forward. They know they have that issue. So what am I going to do? I'm going to try to stay super far back. I'm going to push my hips way far back at the beginning of the squat. And I'm going to squat just way on the back of my heels. But unfortunately, we're not going to be able to get to depth there. And what's going to happen is you're going to lose even more tension and you're going to pop forward just like you otherwise would. So in some cases, this is happening because you're too far back. We have to find that balance before initiating the squat. Balance between the ball of the foot and the heel of the foot. keeping that balance throughout the entire movement, right? It's it's about finding that balance of knees forward versus hips back. We want some of both. We generally want them to happen simultaneously so that that torso angle stays relatively similar throughout the entire movement. A good test and one thing that Taylor likes to do is play your squat in reverse and see if your torso angle on the ascent looks at all similar to your torso angle on the descent. Most of the time, people are going to be here on the descent and here on the ascent. People trying to stay way too upright, worrying about getting pushed forward and then getting pushed forward because they're trying not to get pushed forward. So, embrace the lean a little bit. Find that good balance in forwards and backwards foot pressure. And that's going to be one of the biggest ways that you can train and cue yourself to maintain this posterior chain tension into the bottom and out of the bottom. It's going to make your depth seem better despite not really traveling more range of motion. It's just going to appeal to the rules of powerlifting a little bit better because we're not seeing that knee coming forward. It's staying back. So the knee positionally is staying higher in space, making it easier for your hip crease to get below it. Couple other ways we can work on this. Tempo squats. Tempo squats are great as long as we're maintaining the tempo all the way into the bottom. I think a lot of people mess up tempo squats in the exact same way that I was demonstrating messing up squats. They're good to about halfway or 2/3 and then they kind of speed up and dunk into the bottom. Don't do that in your tempo squats. Extend that tempo. make it smooth all the way through to the very bottom position and it's going to help you fix exactly this. The other thing, the final point here is going to be box squats. Box squats and sitting back. You might hear those things and think those are relics of of the past and of Westside. And I think in a lot of ways in the exaggerated ways that that a lot of that stuff was coached, it is. But I think for lifters who tend to like pop or slide forwards in their squat, box squats can be a really good reminder to reach your hips back. And the way I recommend doing this is setting up something that's far enough behind you that you actually do have to kind of reach for it and not relaxing onto the box. Right? We're not trying to come down and sit onto the box. We're trying to reach back so that we keep our hips and weight back in the bottom and then drive up like you normally would in a squat. We're not trying to relax. We're trying to maintain tension and just use that as an external cue to reach the hips back into the hole. And there you have it. If you've identified this issue in your own squat, or maybe your squat just kind of feels like trash and you don't know why, watch your squat. See if you're doing this. If so, hopefully applying some of the tips I gave in this video helps you to bring it around. Accessory lift number two, accommodating resistance. Number two, deadlift versus bands or chains. Often people will turn to block pulls to try to strengthen the top end of their deadlift, but that cuts out the entire bottom of the range of motion, and I don't think it works very well. Using accommodating resistance allows you to hit the top end of your lift harder without losing the rest of the movement or changing your start position. If you're having a tough time with lockout, bands or chains will both hammer the lockout to make it stronger and help you maintain position off the floor by punishing you for losing that position.
