=== FILE: Struggling with Squat Depth？ You're Bracing Wrong! [-X4RMHlFG18].en.txt ===

If you're having trouble getting to squat depth, you might be thinking to yourself, you know, maybe I'm too tight. Maybe I need to mobilize. I'm here to tell you that probably not. I'm here to tell you that probably what's wrong is your trunk. And I'm going to tell you how to fix it and get to death easier. Spin it more. First, let's take a second and talk about what poor bracing is doing to your squat. When you brace like this with a lot of low back extension and your hips kicked out behind you like that, you're going to get to the bottom and feel like you've run out of room, like you can't possibly go any deeper. And any more depth you do get is probably just going to be from your knees shooting forwards again, making it not look like you're at depth. In order to get to good depth, usually we have to go back to a more neutral looking position, which is going to feel like absolute crap if you've started super extended. What needs to change though is not the position in the bottom, but it's the position throughout the first half of the squat. Proper bracing in our squat is going to look like more of a neutral range back position. We're queuing lifter to kind of pull the ribs down, tuck the pelvis in maybe a little bit. More on that later, but we're trying to achieve something that looks more similar to the bottom position. Even if you brace properly, there's going to be a slight change in your low back and pelvis position to get depth, but we're working to try to minimize that change so that you don't feel as much of a big loss of position and you can be more consistent with your torso and your bracing throughout the entirety of the squat. Okay, so now that you know why you might want to brace like this, let's talk about how you learn to do that and how to integrate it into your squat. I'm going to walk you through it in three parts. Number one, just learning how to do it completely independent of any other movement. So, the cues that I normally walk lifters through are number one to tuck your ribs down into your abs or onto your abs. Number two, to take your usually Lordic lumbar position. This this little bit of extension here. Tuck that in. All right. So, those are the two things. Ribs down, pelvis in. All right. Now, we've got our brace. We should feel a lot of tension and a lot of pressure in the abs and through the obliques. And then we'll breathe into that if we're wearing a belt. Braced. Okay. Now, the next part is taking that brace and incorporating it into movement. In this case, into the hinge. That's where my friend here comes into play. Um, is essentially if your shoulders are better than mine, it'll it'll be a little more comfortable, easy to do. But you want to try to find three points of contact, right? head, upper back, and midback, low back, butt crack. So once you, a more flexible and capable person, have that on your back, you're going to make that same brace position and you're going to hinge. Now, the reason that the the external cue of having the broom handle, mop handle, dowel, whatever, is helpful is because if it comes off of your back, you know that you've broken your position. If when you go to hinge, you start doing this, it's going to come off your midback. If you start doing this or doing this, it's going to come off in different places. So those three points of contact and having that consistent feedback of something touching your back is going to help make sure you don't lose your brace as you go to hinge. So now we've got two of the three parts. We've got our brace, we built it, and we know how to hinge. How do we take that into the squat? Well, all right. So, we've got the bar on our backs. Now, we're going to recreate that hinge position. Normally, a lot of people are squatting like this, right? Chest out, super upright, super extended, we're going to feel super stuck. But with our brand new bracing trick, we're going to pull the ribs down, tuck the hips in, then we're going to hinge to start. And that's why you see a lot of people do what's called the prehinge. It's it's a semi-popular thing that you'll see sometimes in powerlifting. People will lock their brace in, hinge, and then start their squat because that allows them to take their time with arguably the most important and one of the more challenging aspects of starting the squat, which is maintaining the brace while we initiate the squat. Right? So, we're going to brace, ribs down, hips in. Boom. And then there we go. Right. full depth comfortably. No knee sleeves, no weight on the bar, which for an immobile guy like me is a lot. Not once did I have to mobilize to do that. This is going to let you get better depth. If you're getting better depth, your positioning is more consistent. You're going to squat more. You're going to squat more comfortably. you're probably going to maybe get around some discomfort in your hip flexors or your low back or your upper back because you're going to be in a position that's a little bit more natural for you to get to good depth. Relying on that prehinge every time can kind of lead to more issues. So over time, you want to transition from the really distinct two-step squat where you prehinge and then squat into just being able to walk the bar out with something similar to your starting torso angle and then go into the squat. Right? You want to be able to make that a bit of a smoother transition because anytime you lock out a squat, if you're doing the prehinge, you're going to lock out a squat, have to hinge, and then do it. and you're just going to be doing a whole lot of weird little movements that maybe are unnecessary. It also can maybe mess with your balance a little bit if you hinge too far forward or hinge too far back. But again, practice it and that should fix things up for you. The lifter on the right here is utilizing what I would consider a more proper brace, a more neutral range position in the low back and hips and is smoothly and seamlessly getting to depth, squatting comfortably, seeing minimal change in their position into and out of the hole. What's going on, guys? Welcome back to Calgary Barb. Today, we're going to go over one of my absolute favorite deadlift accessory movements. I think it's probably if I if I could only do one deadlift accessory movement other than a competition deadlift, this would be it. And we're going to go over the pause deadlift today. So, the first thing I want to talk about with the pause deadlift is why would we want to do this movement? The reason it's so valuable is because it essentially forces you to start the lift twice. Uh it really really reinforces the bottom position and how to maintain proper positioning off the floor because if positioning alters that much between the first position being on the floor and the and the pause position being maybe an inch off the floor then that's when you're going to start to see a lot of the technical breakdowns that lead to a slow lock out or problematic lockout positioning. Now, if anybody is listen if you guys have listened to me coach the deadlift at all, I'm very very big on starting position and maintaining that position. And that is why this movement is so valuable. Second, how do we do this movement? Essentially, what you're going to do is you're going to start the deadlift. You're going to pause about an inch to 2 in off the floor and then you're going to complete the movement. Uh we want to be paused for maybe a second to two seconds, about a two count usually. Now, third, we're going to go over some common mistakes. The biggest mistakes I see are either rushing the pause. Uh, another mistake that I see often is going to be losing position from the floor to the pause position. The third and more subtle mistake that I see sometimes is people going from a push to a pull too early. Now, to explain that, what we want is we want to start the movement with a push. Now, this is regardless of whether you're pulling sumo or conventional. We're starting the deadlift with a push. As far as I'm concerned, we want to go from a push to the pause about an inch to two inches off the floor. And then we want to push again to restart and reinitiate the lift. my way to chin-ups so I also wanted to use this as an opportunity to talk a little bit about how and why I use D loads and how Mike programs D loads for me as well so in the sort of strategy of training that we're using right now we have a focused developmental block where most of the work is going in all the heavy stuff where we're pushing the weights up and striving to get stronger and achieve certain adaptations from the lifter and we've also timed that so it's a specific length that's specific to the lifter and we run the cycle for that length and then we do a washout and then we run another cycle and it's a very sort of phasic structure in that sense when we do a washout there are two main things that we're looking for number one we're looking to eliminate or dissipate as much fatigue as we can and prepare the lifter for the next phase as well we're looking to lose as little strength as possible so in some cases depending on the length of the peak will often alter the length of the washout because if we wash out too long after a short period of developmental phase then we're gonna start losing some of the adaptation that we'd gained so we'll often tailor the length of the washout to the length of the developmental phase those two will be tied together now traditionally when people deal owed a lot of people think okay well I'm going to deal owed I'm going to remove some of the intensity from this program we're gonna trim the volume back and in most cases I think that's sort of how people think about a traditional D load but a lot of the times since working with Mike and in my own programming now we'll often deal owed in specificity as well so what we'll do is we'll choose very nonspecific movements that will target similar muscle groups similar movement patterns but are far enough removed from the competition movement that we're going to be able to push them hopefully maintaining some of that strength but at the same time because it's so nonspecific we're able to dissipate some of that fatigue a lot of times you're usually not very good at them because they're so nonspecific there's stuff that you don't normally see in your developmental blocks and that can lend itself to still making sure that things are very challenging so throughout these phases you'll often see high reps nonspecific movements and sort of tied in with the high reps is gonna be lower weight so I hope that's provided some insight into how and why I D load and how Mike programs D loads for myself if you guys have any comments or questions about === FILE: The Beginner Secret： Why Linear Progression Works [D97OJAFrkPE].en.txt ===

So, the first of these progression models we're going to look at is what's called linear progression. Now, linear progression dictates that pretty much every time you do a session or week to week even, you're just going to add weight. And presumably that's going to work for quite a while when you're a beginner because not only are you going to adapt quickly cuz this these are stimuli that you maybe never experienced before, but also you're developing on multiple levels. You're going to be developing in terms of putting on muscle, putting on strength and the coordination that's necessary to do movements like squatting, benching, and deadlifting. Those adaptations are going to happen fast. Therefore, you'll be able to just add weight pretty much every time you approach the bar. Number go up. That is the crux of a linear progression. If you're doing a 3x5 or a 5x5 and your plan is just add weight each time, that's your classic linear progression. You're going to make gains quite quickly, meaning you will have adapted and likely recovered by the time your next session rolls around, hence the ability to add weight. After a period of time though, this stops working as

=== FILE: The Bench Press J-Curve： Why You NEED It [Ocgqs9dQ9cU].en.txt ===

Cool cut. In that last segment, you would have seen one of our app members, Marsha, demonstrating her previous bench press faults. Now you can see clearly that as she comes off the chest, elbows flare, shoulders lose position, bar goes the opposite way. Now I'm going to break it down here and try to demonstrate it as well. So what we tend to see is one of two things. Either we're losing position as we get to the chest and the elbows are coming out behind the bar so that when we press up, the bar naturally goes away from us. or we get down to the chest, we're in good position all the way through and then when we go to press, the shoulders slide up out of position and again elbows end up behind the bar and we kind of press the bar out away from ourselves. Now, a lot of lifters, especially on heavy attempts, you'll notice they come straight up and out a little bit, it stalls, and then they're able to bring it back. And as they bring it back, things speed through. But ideally, the skill we're looking to develop in the bar path that we want to see is that we touch the chest. We bring the bar slightly back and up. So the immediate movement off the chest is back and then up. It's like a little J shape, little J curve bar path. For some lifters, this J curve is going to be really pronounced and you'll be able to easily trace it even just watching. Other lifters, it'll be a little more subtle. But if you can get this slight back over the shoulders bench bar path to happen, you're going to be more consistent and more better more more better better leveraged in your bench us.

Accessory lift one, deficit deadlifts. First up, deficit deadlifts. Now, these can be pretty brutal, and honestly, I'd only recommend them for conventional deadlifters, not as a sumo accessory. But by extending the range of motion and putting yourself up on a 1 to 2 in block, you can really build a lot of strength in the first few inches of the lift and teach yourself to be patient and stay tight while you're breaking the bar off the floor. I wouldn't go any bigger than a maybe two 3inch deficit at most. And I also wouldn't go down to an inch or a half inch deficit cuz I think that's just going to mess with your usual pattern. We want this to be distinct enough that it actually trains something differently.

=== FILE: The Complete Guide to a Stronger Deadlift Grip [L8aR5QoXSIk].txt ===

 Welcome back to Calgary Barbell. My name is Bryce, and I'm here to fix your deadlift. In powerlifting, nothing is more frustrating than being strong enough to lock out a deadlift, but your grip giving up. This has cost people PRs and championships and records, and honestly, it just kind of sucks. If you're struggling with your deadlift grip, then look no further. Today's video is going to cover everything that I've amassed throughout my career in lifting, and that includes the strength to hold onto a 400kg deadlift, as well as the protocols I've used with multiple world level lifters now to take their grip strength to the next level. Now there are two ways of gripping the bar for deadlifts. The key to either of these grips is that they stop the bar from rolling out of your hands. Option A is a mixed grip, option B is a hook grip. With a mixed grip, here's the low down. When you're setting up for a mixed grip, one hand goes under and one hand goes over. There will be one of these orientations that will feel quite a bit more comfortable than the other, so try a few either way to get a sense for which of those works for you. The reason this stops the bar from rolling is because if it rolls out of one hand, in theory, it is rolling into the other hand. If you want to perfect a mixed grip in the deadlift, then focus on these three things. Thing number one, pull the slack out of your grip. The same way we pull the slack out of the bar, the same way we set all of our tension before we initiate the deadlift itself, we want to do the same thing with the grip. Now what the heck does that mean? What that means is get the bar to essentially the lowest point of your grip and the highest point of resistance before you pull. If you're setting the bar really high up in your hands and wrapping more of your hand and fingers around it, it's going to roll some when you start. Now this rolling counteracts the entire purpose behind the mixed grip, which is to stop the bar from rolling. Once this rolling happens, if it occurs at any point through the lift, it is going to feel bad and it is going to make you not deadlift as well or not be able to deadlift as much weight. Thing number two, pick a side. Now like I said earlier, one orientation of over versus under will feel better and more natural than the other. Go with it. Don't worry about trying to switch it up for your warm-up sets or on secondary days. If you're worried about quote unquote imbalances or shoulder health or something like that, there are ways to address that. However, what we're talking about in this video is how to efficiently grip for the deadlift, which is a skill and requires repetition to practice. If you're changing your grip orientation constantly from session to session, it's going to be really hard to get those reps and that practice for the skill of deadlifting. Thing number three, let them hang. Now what I mean by that is I see people over tax their grip because they're trying to pull the bar. They're trying to be far too active with their grip and their arms and they're not thinking about their hands as just hooks. We want a good solid grip. We want to squeeze the hands, but we also need to be somewhat passive. We don't want to be bending at the elbows and trying to pull with the biceps. We're going to put probably too much pressure on the biceps and the pecs if we get into that habit. So we really want to try to anchor things in the shoulder blade, keep the arms nice and long and keep that pressure tight, but passive in the grip. Now if instead you are a hook grip enjoyer like myself, here's the lowdown. So we are essentially just wedging our thumb in there and squeezing the crap out of it. I want to add that I don't accept that this only works for people with freakishly long digits. Now a couple quick notes about setup. When we're wedging the thumb in there, we want to internally rotate at the shoulders to give ourselves a little bit more length of thumb to grab onto. However, once we start pulling the slack, we want to externally rotate and put our shoulders back into the position where we're going to get a little more out of the upper back. This is also going to bring the thumb parallel to not perpendicular to the bar. And when you're grabbing your thumb, you want to try to line it up so your middle finger in the most distal knuckle grabs onto the nail bed of your thumb and your pointer finger will overlap the knuckle of the thumb. The other two fingers kind of don't really do too much. Here are my three tips for a perfect hook grip. Thing number one, it takes two. Now what I mean here is like I was saying, generally the hook grip is going to come down to two fingers. That's kind of all that you really need to anchor on the thumb to have a solid hook grip. If you're mucking up your positioning so that you can get more than those two fingers onto your thumb, you're probably doing yourself a disservice and creating a less sturdy grip at the end of the day. Thing number two, pull the slack out of your grip as well. Just like we said, with the mixed grip, we want to make sure that the bar is settled, that your grip is solid as hell before you start pulling. It's easier, I think, with hook grip to take too deep of a grip and have a bit of a roll to the bar feel kind of natural at the beginning of your deadlift. Don't do that. Make sure that the bar is as low as it's going to go so the bar is not rolling against you when you're pulling 300 plus kilos or whatever. Thing number three, preserve your thumb skin. Now, not everybody has to be quite as reserved with their hook grip as I am, but I think if you're trying to hook grip every single set, every single rep and high rep sets in particular, you're probably going to end up tearing and damaging your thumb webbing, which is just going to prevent you from being able to actually train your grip. So what I recommend is taking your top set or sets with hook grip. I generally won't do more than maybe a triple with hook grip. If we're pushing into sets of four and up, if we are doing a whole bunch of volume in our back offs, a lot of the time that's a great place to use straps fairly liberally. I use straps even when I'm warming up and in my peaking blocks, a lot of the times I'll do about three singles a week and the rest of my work is all strapped up. Luckily, as a hook grip, enjoyer, the feeling of pulling into position and the actual distance of the bar from you and all of these kinds of things can be very similar between pulling with straps and pulling with hook grip. If you're looking for an extra set of eyes on your deadlifts for your grip or maybe on any other lift in terms of helping you correct some technical mistakes, well, you can check out the Calgary Barbell training app where you get access to over 50 programs as well as expert coaching from real people, including myself and the team here at Calgary Barbell each week in our app members discord. If that's something that sounds interesting to you and you want to take your training to the next level, then check the link in the description below or go to calgarybarbell.com for more details. Part two, grip training. If you're somebody who's watching this video and you have the grip fundamentals down but for whatever reason it still starts to fall apart when you approach a max load, we've got you covered. This is Britney Schlater and this is Oliver Dahlquist. What do these two have in common? Well, they're both wonderful people and they're both very strong. They've both meddled at IPF world level competitions and they've both broken world records. But they also both used to struggle with their deadlift grip, that is until we put in a whole bunch of work and they got substantially better. So how do we do that? First, we just add holds to our existing deadlift training on the last rep of the last set and on the last rep of any top set or top single. We're just going to hold for four to six seconds. It doesn't have to be anything crazy. It doesn't have to be a 30 second hold. Just hold what you're already doing for a little bit longer, but do that every time that you do it. And the second thing we'll do is introduce high rack pulls or block pulls. Please for the love of God, do not submit good competition bars to rack pulls. If you have a nice bar, only do block pulls. If you have an old beat up crappy bar that you don't care about bending the hell out of, then you can go ahead and do rack pulls. But the idea here is that once we're done our main deadlifts on our main deadlift day, we're going to haul the bar and all the plates over to somewhere where we can set up a high rack or block pull. Something where we can get to lock out within two to three inches of range of motion. Then we're going to do some pick and holds. We're going to start with 80 to 85% of our one rep max. We're going to hold for eight to 10 seconds each set. And we're going to do three sets of this. Simply pick the bar like you would if you were doing a deadlift, lock it out all the way and hold it there. Don't let yourself rest on your thighs. Just a quick aside there. Each week you do these, try to add a little bit of weight. If the time you can hold it for goes down, then stay at that weight for another couple weeks until you can get the time back up. Just progress this along and between those two protocols, I promise you. You will put a whole bunch more weight in your hands and hold on to it better than you have before. And that's our video for today. Thank you for watching. Hopefully this helps you hold on to more deadlifts and get more white lights and hit more PRs and break a record and whatever else. If you enjoyed the video, make sure to let us know. If you have other grip training things that you've tried and that have helped you maybe share it in the comments below so that more people can do better at things. Yeah, thanks for watching. Like and subscribe. We'll see you in the next one. Bye-bye.

=== FILE: The Long Pause Bench： Underrated Strength Builder [i-ylz1zdp5s].en.txt ===

Let's start off with one of my favorite movements that highlights something that lifters mess up all of the time. The long pause bench press. If you want to build a big bench, you've got to be strong and skilled while the bar is on your chest. Many raw lifters think that their lockout is their weakness when in actuality what happens is they lose position either while touching their chest or while pressing off of the chest. Long pause bench is a classic and it's in damn near every program that I write. Get better at pausing, get better at benching. If we can be stronger in that bottom position and in breaking inertia, we're going to put kilos on the bench. Period. You never heard period? No. No. I'll usually program these for no more than about four reps and no less than about a seven RP because we want some intensity and we want some specificity on this movement. I'll also differentiate between a twocount pause bench and a 3ount pause bench. Often swapping between those in programming. So the key to long pause bench is to make sure that the bar is motionless. No bounce, no momentum during the pause. And be careful at how quickly you count. Every single week, I remind lifters that their long pauses need to be longer.

=== FILE: The Proper Way to Load Your Plates [X0hui2Sb5FE].en.txt ===

So, maybe it's your first time at a powerlifting gym. You want to look like you know what you're doing. You want to fit in with the cool kids. Powerlifters, most of them aren't cool, so don't worry about that. If you want to impress everybody, just put the plates on the bar like this. The first plate always faces in. The rest of the plates always face out. It's a tiny little thing. It is a rule technically in the rule book so that you can see the branding and so you can more easily tell what weight is on the bar if you're in the referee's chair. Maybe there's some other reasons for it. If you load your bar like that, everybody's going to be like, "Yo, that person knows what they're doing." And then you're in.

=== FILE: The Right Way to Program Squat Accessories #powerlifting #squats [F7k9xCchtYQ].en.txt ===

Like we said in the deadlift video, you don't want to do all five of these at once, nor do you want to be changing them up every single week. Pick one or two that you think apply to your specific needs and weaknesses in your training. Run them for a period of time. Assess whether or not they helped. Either run them again or change them in the next block. For most lifters, I would say you can probably run two of these as well as a comp squat each week. I think most lifters squat frequency can be a little bit higher than their deadlift frequency. So, I think if you were to run a paused squat and a tempo squat, or a pin squat and a paused squat, or any combination of those, you'd probably be just fine.

=== FILE: The Ultimate Powerlifting Meet Warm-Up Guide (Squat, Bench, Deadlift) [AzZxvP3liKE].en.txt ===

Nothing tests your strength quite like a powerlifting meet. But how do you ensure that your performance reflects what you're truly capable of? In today's video, we're going to take you through the timing, the process, and the intricacies of warming up for a powerlifting competition so that you're ready when it comes time to step on the platform. Welcome to episode 6 of the Path of Powerlifting series. In our last video, we left off at what we call the lull of a powerlifting meet. So, at this point, you've gone through the pre-meat process and you're waiting to get warmed up. But first, you'll need to know what sessions and flights are. A session is a group of flights, and a flight is a group of lifters. A session can have up to three flights, and a flight can contain up to 14 lifters. All lifters from the same session will weigh in at the same time. Your flight list should be posted at weigh-ins, so check it out to find out which flight you'll be lifting in. You need to know this because your flight will determine when you start warming up. If you're flight A, you'll start warming up about 30 to 40 minutes before the scheduled start time of the session. If you're in flight B, you're going to start warming up when flight A starts their attempts or very shortly before. And if you're in flight C, you'll start warming up around the time flight B starts their attempts. You'll likely need to share a rack with one or more people for your warm-ups. Don't be shy. Approach a rack. Ask, "How many people are on the rack and whereabouts are you opening?" Ideally, you don't want to share a rack that already has five or more people on it or a rack with somebody who's way stronger or way taller than you are. But you don't always get the choice. You know who I would share a rack with though? Canadian powerlifting legends Ryan and Reyes Stin. I like them. I like powerlifting and so do they. Which is why their company Innerstrength Products.ca has partnered with us to bring you this in-depth educational resource. Inner Strength has anything and everything you need to get started in powerlifting. It's a Canadian company and it's run by some of the realest lifters and people in the game. and I I can't exclaim proudly enough how happy we are to work with them on this project. So, head over to innerstrengthproducts.ca the next time you need pretty much anything and support those who support powerlifting. A lot of people will bring someone with them to help out on meet day, whether it's just a friend or a full-blown game day coach. Ideally, if you're bringing somebody to help you out at your first powerlifting meet, they're somebody who has experience with the gym or better yet with powerlifting. And if the person you're bringing doesn't have that experience, definitely send them this video or some of the others in the Path of Powerlifting series so they have a primer and know a little more about what to expect. Whoever this person is, they should be ready to load and unload plates in the warm-up room. The lifter should not have to do this. Coaches and handlers should help each other out on the rack as well. Your handler should be communicating with other coaches and handlers to at the very least load, unload, and adjust bar height for all lifters in the rack. Now, let's talk about the actual warm-ups themselves. In the description box below, you can grab the warm-up and attempt selection sheet that I made years ago that myself and the other Calgary barbell coaches still use to this day. So, open the Google Drive link and make a copy so you can edit it and then you can follow along. The numbers that the sheet spits out are the approximate warm-ups that I use taken as a percentage of your goal third attempt. The percentages are as follows. Warm up one is the bar for five to eight reps. Warm up two, 30% for five reps. Warm up three, 45% for three reps. Warm up four, 60% for a single. Warm up five, 72% for a single. And warm up six, 82% for a single. A quick consideration here, for everything except maybe your last one or two singles in your warm-up, just round it to the nearest 5 kilo increment so it's easier for everybody to load and unload. For example, if you're warming up to a 200 kilo opener, you don't need to take 67.5 as your first warm-up just because that's what the sheets spit out. Take 70. Bear in mind that any of the suggestions that the sheet makes are just that, suggestions. Any of the numbers on this sheet, attempts included, are just a starting point and a guideline. Once you've got your warm-up weights, we need to then figure out your warm-up timing. What I recommend is moving really quickly through your first three warm-ups. There's no need to rest any more than it takes to get the bar loaded and rotate through the lifters on your rack. what's going on everybody welcome back to Calgary barbell today we're gonna bring you some tips for your benchpress now these are a little bit unconventional but one of the things that I think a lot our fingers so you can see here the bars too high up in our fingers and we have a huge amount of distance between where the bar rests and where the force is going to come through the end of the forearm so it's a big energy leak now the other way people might try to fix that is by trying to have more neutral wrists but you can see there that puts the bar out in front of my elbow makes it very hard for me to try to keep my elbows in under the bar so one of two things is gonna happen either we're gonna be back behind the bar and end up pushing the bar away off the chest or the wrists are  aposin, Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing-r Standing Standing-r Standing Standing-r Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing Standing sort of rotation you can get when you take the grip on the bar. The sort of bulldog or sometimes called Japanese grip versus a more conventional sort of straight on grip to the bar. But what I want to talk about today is actually how deep the bar is in your hands. Now I think the mistake a lot of people make is that they take the bar for the bench press like they would for the deadlift. So it's further down towards the fingertips and this causes a couple of things we're going to show in just a second here. My big tip, my recommendation here is to work on taking the grip lower in your palm. Now you may be or may know lifters who are a lot more comfortable with what's called a false grip where the thumb is behind the bar instead of laid over the bar. What I'm recommending here is we try to sort of meld the two. The reason people like a false grip is because it puts the bar more directly over the wrist and allows us to kind of set it and forget it when it comes to grip. We're not thinking about stabilizing the wrists because we put it in a natural position where it just sits and then we worry about elbow position, shoulder position, etc. which is another video. So the way we're going to place the bar, the way I recommend to place the bar is actually to kind of push the thumb out of the way so that we can get the bar set on the meat of the palm right into the sort of the butt of the hand we'll call it and that's going to allow you to stack it right over the wrist and then we're going to fold or lay the fingers down across the bar. You can see there's actually a little gap here between my knuckles and sort of the first digit of my fingers and the bar. So we're more worried about getting that bar low in the hand than we are about having a super sort of contactful grip with the bar. We're laying the fingers down across it. Now let's show you why we might want the bar lower in the palm. Now I want to demonstrate from a practical standpoint what the what taking the bar lower in the palm is going to do for you. So to illustrate that what I'm going to show is first off what happens when we take the bar too high up in our fingers. So you can see here the bar is too high up in our fingers and we have a huge amount of distance between where the bar rests and where the force is going to come through the end of the forearm. So it's a big energy leak. Now the other way people might try to fix that is by trying to have more neutral wrists. But you can see there that puts the bar out in front of my elbow makes it very hard for me to try to keep my elbows in under the bar. So one of two things is going to happen either we're going to be back behind the bar and end up pushing the bar away off the chest or the wrists are going to cock back anyways and then we're going to be back in that same crappy position. So by taking the bar lower in the palms it allows us to set a certain angle in the wrist which is going to keep the bar relatively over the top of the forearm and allow us to keep the elbows in line underneath or just slightly in front of the bar. So we have better control over the bar path it's easier to press the bar back over the shoulders as we go through the movement and we're a little bit more sturdy as opposed to having to try to fight for an angle in the wrist that is not going to be maintainable. Now obviously these tips are not necessarily going to work for every single person but it is something I would recommend you at least try and see if it affects your bench press in a positive way. goal-setting is going to be to set moderately difficult but realistic goals the reason we want things to be moderately difficult in terms of our goals is we want them to motivate us we want our goals to force us to push harder to do more work to be mindful of the process but we don't want it to be so hard that we can't get there because then it becomes frustrating and unmotivated and on the flip third principle is to set each of all the three types of goals that's gonna be outcome goals performance goals and process goals outcome goals are goals that are focused on a competitive outcome these and see that honestly I wasn't even really that far off by the end of the block lastly but definitely not least are the process goals now these the goals that are focused on all of the actions that === FILE: This Is Why Your Deadlift Feels So Hard [s_WlMhvwdes].txt ===

 If you are struggling to progress your deadlift, and it looks like this, this, this, or like this, then you're making the same mistake as the rest of these lifters, and that's probably why it's stuck. Now, this mistake isn't just limited to beginners either. Check this out. This lifter here is pulling 285 kilos and same mistake. So what's happening here? Well, all of these deadlifts are more of a pull than a push. And when we pull deadlifts, what ends up happening is we use a lot more of our back than we need to, and we're not using our quads. If we watch Aaron's deadlift here, there's a little dip before the pull, but then his hips shoot right back up, and he ends up pretty much stiff-legging it. Now, both Josh and Owen here just start with very high hips, meaning they're not able to get their hips into a position where the quads can contribute much. And Johannes here is somewhere in between. We do pull in at least just a bit, but we're not pulling in all the weight. There isn't enough tension, or anything. enough of a push. So how do we fix it? It's not as simple as just sit your hips lower. We have to learn how to build tension before we start the lift. In order to find tension, find your appropriate position, and use your quads properly in the deadlift, I like to do this quick little checklist when I set up for the pull. Number one, heels, hips, and hammies. Push your weight way back on your heels until you find tension in your hips and hamstrings. Number two, lats. Pull your arms long and tighten your lats and resist the weight of the bar with your upper back. Number three, find your quads. Keeping all that other tension, literally use the weight of the bar to pull your hips down until we find pressure through the whole foot and you feel your quads light up. Once you've got that tension, when you're starting the lift, be patient. Fixing this issue is going to make your deadlift feel a little bit harder off the floor. That's a good thing, though. If you're not used to this position, your body will probably still try to kick your hips up and force you to stiff-legged. Making big adjustments to your technique like this can be pretty tricky. That's why we put so much emphasis on exactly that in the Calgary Barbell Training App. We do weekly video check-ins to help our lifters refine their technique so they're more efficient and they get stronger faster. If you'd prefer to roll the dice and potentially be selected for me to look at in one of these videos, we pull a few submissions from our inbox each month and you could submit your videos at calgarybarbell.com. And if your deadlift looks like one of those deadlifts from the videos at the start, well, make sure that you're finding tension before you start the lift. That's going to help you fix your position. It's going to allow you to use your quads and to push, not pull your deadlift. If you can fix that, you're going to feel a lot better real fast.

=== FILE: This Is Why the Bar Feels Heavy on Your Back [ZKbogyX7QgQ].en.txt ===

Mistake number two, improper upper back positioning. A lot of lifters will struggle with creating a good shelf for the bar to rest on when squatting. And my tip here is that we need some degree of pulling the shoulder blades back and down to create that shelf. If you look at more novice lifters, a lot of them will be shrugged up in the shoulder blades and maybe even pushed forwards in the shoulder blades. This can result in them having issues with their wrists and elbows and shoulders in terms of discomfort and also in being bullied around by the bar. We need to be tight and rigid in the upper back in what I call the shelf in order to have a good squat. So, make sure that we're creating tension in the upper back and using that to tie the bar into our aforementioned brace.

=== FILE: This Might Be Why Your Lifts Aren’t Improving… [mBZ9UR2gDOo].en.txt ===

I am a scientist. Well, no, actually I'm not, but I am a pretty good lifter and a good coach. Now, with this sheer volume of lifting advice out there, it can be hard to know for yourself what technique advice should I follow. So today we're going to use a very straightforward and simple take loosely based on the scientific method to help you individualize and assess lifting advice. Step zero, what do you want to change? In order for this whole process to work properly, you need to come up with a guiding question or a hypothesis. And it can be as simple as asking, will making this change make me stronger? But the more general the question, the harder it is to answer with any certainty. If your question is more specific, like, will insert Q here help my squat depth? Then we're more likely to arrive at a helpful conclusion. First and foremost, we have to compare apples to apples. You're going to basically be a scientist here, eliminating variables and having a control set and an experimental set. Step one, isolate the variables and test. Here's an example. We're going to load 75% of your one rep max. Then we're going to perform some sets of 3 to five reps. Keep the rep number the same across each of those sets. For the first set, just perform the set as you normally would. This is your control set. On the second set, this is your experimental set where you're going to make whatever adjustments you want to investigate. For example, if you're playing with a heavier touch on your bench press, this second set is where you test that. Now, make sure to film both sets from the same angle, though. A quick note, if you're investigating multiple different changes to your lift, try not to incorporate more than one queue per experimental set. If you're changing too many of those variables at once, you can muddy the waters. And then if a set goes especially well or poorly, you might have a hard time deciphering which of those changed variables produce that outcome. Step two, assess the differences. After we've performed our control and experimental sets, we need to have a criteria for evaluating them. Here are some example questions you could ask yourself. What feedback did you get in terms of how the bar speed was? Which set was more comfortable? Did we hit better depth or pause better? Was the lockout cleaner? These questions should be guided by your original hypothesis and help to answer whether or not the cues that you implemented had the impact that you desire. I also recommend that you record the answers to these questions after each set. It may also be the case that you're testing something that will require a longer period of time to assess. For example, will switching to sumo deadlift make me stronger? With a more general question like this, you'll need to assess it over a longer period of time. There's also a case to be made that with any of these cues or technical changes to lifts that you should assess it over a period of a few backto-back blocks as opposed to just a couple of single sets. You will, of course, have to use some critical thinking skills to determine what's right for you. Let's face it, being objective about all of these things in your own training is difficult. That's why it can help immensely to get a professional involved. If you want help assessing your technique, we've built the Calgary barbell training app to help with exactly that. In our app, we do weekly video technique reviews for our lifters. Plus, we've got a pretty incredible app exclusive Discord community. And on top of that, we've got 50 plus programs to run for lifters of all experience levels and varying goals. But don't just take our word for it. This is Blaine. Blaine's one of our longtime app members and in 9 months Blaine PR his comp total by 50 kilos. He squatted 277 and a half, benched 170, and deadlifted 260. Blaine is just one of hundreds of lifters who have benefited hugely from the app. And if you're interested, you can check it out at calgary barbell.com. Step three, keep what works, ditch what doesn't. There are so many cues out there. And as a coach, I've got a pretty robust collection of cues, sometimes even multiple cues, to try to get the same technique outcome from a lifter. It's important to learn to filter things, especially once we start this process of analyzing and changing our technique. There are instances where we might want to keep a queue that didn't feel great right away. for example, if it allows us to get better squat depth. But in most cases, if a Q doesn't produce some kind of benefit, be it stability, strength, or comfort, right away, we should just move on from it. We also want to be careful that we don't go making sweeping changes to our technique every single time we've had a bad or an off session. Lifters will often think, "Oh man, my bench was so bad on Wednesday. I must have to make some technical changes." without considering that maybe they just had a bad day. To help you avoid this before trying to experiment with your technique, ask yourself, has this been an issue for more than just a block or two? Am I confident that my recovery and fatigue management outside of the gym is in a good place? Am I using intelligently designed programming? You should be able to confirm that each of these things is taken care of before you start overanalyzing a technique that's potentially already working for you. Step four, distill it down. If we find some cues that work well, then we need to have a way to integrate them into the technique without needing a full paragraph you're trying to think through while unrackcking the bar. Often when thinking about queuing, we end up with things like pull your elbows in or ribs down, which aren't bad starting points, but we need to start learning how to turn these cues into things that we can feel. When trying to implement a queue, we don't necessarily want to be thinking about how a thing looks because when we're lifting, we don't have direct visual feedback, especially if you plan to compete in powerlifting. Ideally, we can translate these verbal cues into sensations that have immediate feedback. How does it feel to lock your lats or shoulder blades down? Try and create that sensation before you get under the bar so that we're not trying to translate words into visuals and then visuals into movement. We do however want some visual feedback. But to get this, we need to perform and film the set and then review that. This process is the creation of what I call cornerstone cues. Cornerstone cues are simple, just one word or even sometimes a concept that makes all of the other more complex cues fall into place. For me, on my bench, I know that I need to find my leg tightness and find a specific feeling in my shoulder blades. So, my cornerstone cues are feet, shoulders. In my squat, I know that I need to have a really tight brace and get my upper back set before I pick up the bar. So cornerstone cues for the squat are brace lats. When we get under 100 plus% of our max, we need to have small reliable cues that are meaningful in a big way. The cues that we keep and stick with should take minimal brain power. And if we've done a good job of creating sensations associated with those cues, then we can implement them quickly and seamlessly. Note that this process of examination and elimination can be used for any number of changes that you might like to make. Be it new shoes, new sleeves, or anything else you'd like to try out. All right. Now, I know we may have veered a little bit from the science, and to be fair, the association was loose at best. I really just wanted to say I am a scientist and wear a lab coat in this video. But hopefully some of the information in this video helps you create a process whereby you can evaluate some of the overabundant lifting and technique advice out there. === FILE: This Old Cue Is Messing Up Your Squat [6lCplkKnpP4].en.txt ===

Mistake number three, driving your chest up. There used to for a long time, especially when I first got into powerlifting, be a very prevalent cue. Lifters should drive their chest up when squatting that once you hit the hole, just just push your chest up, reach your chest up. This is maybe one of the worst cues out there. Now, I don't think it's as prevalent anymore, and this kind of does double back on or piggyback on the bracing queue, but a lot of lifters will hit the bottom and then try to drive their chest up to ensure that they're not getting pulled forward by the bar. In actuality, like I said previously, this is going to mess with our brace. So, what we need to be doing in the squat is when we hit the bottom, we need to be keeping those ribs down and being patient out of the bottom. The first portion of the lift where we drive out of the hole, we should be focusing on maintaining the brace and pushing with the legs really hard. That way, we're setting ourselves up to be stronger and better positioned for the second and third/ thirds of the lift.

=== FILE: Top 5 Accessory Movements for a Massive Deadlift (That Actually Work) [L4VQM_yd4nM].en.txt ===

So, you want a bigger deadlift. You and every other lifter on the planet. But if all you're doing is straight deadlifts from the floor, you might be leaving some gains on the table. So, what I'm going to do is take you through five of my favorite accessory movements, slight variations on the deadlift that could help you target your weak points, fix patterns that maybe are holding you back, and build some more muscle so you can have a massive deadlift. The deadlift is a pretty complex sum of a whole bunch of little parts, right? We've got our grip strength, we've got our leg strength, back strength, timing, positioning, all that stuff rolled into one. If your deadlift is stalling, there's a decent chance one or some of those components is falling behind. Choosing the right accessory movement can help you emphasize different aspects of the deadlift, fix technique, bring up legging muscle groups, and overall just build a big old deadlift. There is no reason to be alive if you can't do deadlifts. Accessory lift one, deficit deadlifts. First up, deficit deadlifts. Now, these can be pretty brutal, and honestly, I'd only recommend them for conventional deadlifters, not as a sumo accessory. But by extending the range of motion and putting yourself up on a 1 to two inch block, you can really build a lot of strength in the first few inches of the lift. And teach yourself to be patient and stay tight while you're breaking the bar off the floor. I wouldn't go any bigger than a maybe 2 3in deficit at most. And I also wouldn't go down to an inch or a/ in deficit cuz I think that's just going to mess with your usual pattern. We want this to be distinct enough that it actually trains something differently. Quick tip for your deficit deadlift. You're either going to have to pull with your hips a fair bit higher than you normally would in your competition lift or pull with your hips a lot lower than you would in your competition lift. If you're a lifter whose hips tend to shoot up when you start your comp deadlift, definitely get those hips down. work on emphasizing that patience and keeping the hips low as you start. If you're not a lifter who has that issue, just go with the higher hip wedge and you'll be fine. Accessory lift number two, accommodating resistance. Number two, deadlift versus bands or chains. Often people will turn to block pulls to try to strengthen the top end of their deadlift, but that cuts out the entire bottom of the range of motion, and I don't think it works very well. Using accommodating resistance allows you to hit the top end of your lift harder without losing the rest of the movement or changing your start position. If you're having a tough time with lockout, bands or chains will both hammer the lockout to make it stronger and help you maintain position off the floor by punishing you for losing that position. All right, so not every gym is going to have access to bands and chains, but if you do, here's how to set them up quick and how much to use. First, let's talk about bands. If you have dumbbells, set one in front of the platform, one behind the platform. Maybe toss some fat grips on there if there's nurling to protect the band. Just loop it around underneath the dumbbell, obviously, across and back. Boom. If you don't have dumbbells and all you have is a band, you can drape it over the bar like so. Stand on it, and then let it rip. If you're pulling sumo, you can do the same thing. set it in a little narrower. You'll have to stretch the band out a little, maybe just straight up and down like so. And then you can pull sumo against bands like that. For chains, if you're pulling sumo, just drape them right over the middle of the bar. What I like to do, I it's weird, but I like to get a dish cloth and set it over the center nurling so the chains don't muck up the bar. If you're pulling conventional, that's not going to work. So, you'll need to put the chains on the outside. Try to put them as far out this way as possible so the bar doesn't land on them. Quick tip there. And how much to use? Well, go buy yourself a fish scale off of Amazon for N bucks. You can use this, hold it at the top about where lockout's going to be to measure the resistance you're getting from either the chains or the bands and use anywhere from 10 to 20% of your one rep max on the deadlift. Third, the Romanian deadlift. There's a reason bodybuilders use these to beat the piss out of their hamstring. They're really good at targeting the posterior chain, hamstrings, glutes, spinal erectors. But the flip side is that you're also going to get way better at hinging. And the hinge pattern is super central to the deadlift and to the squat to some extent. Building stronger hamstrings and perfecting your hinge in the deadlift is super important because that's going to allow you to really be in the position you want to be in once that bar comes past the knees and also it's going to strengthen your lock out. Okay, so the first thing I want to do here is differentiate the Romanian deadlift from the stiff-legged deadlift. A Romanian deadlift is going to start from the top. It starts with the eccentric or lowering phase. You're going to go down just past the knees and come back up. That's one rep. Picking the bar up doesn't count as a rep. A stiff leg deadlift, you're going to start from a dead stop every time. You're going to go all the way to the floor. You're going to keep your hips much, much higher with less knee bend. This is your start position for a stiff leg. When you're doing a Romanian deadlift, you want to try to find a good balance between pressure on your heels. So we can feel a lot of good hamstring stretch and tension and allowing the knees to come forwards enough that by the time the bar gets to the bottom, we are getting a little bit of that quad feeling and a little bit of that push to start the lift. That way it's going to carry over better into your deadlift and help with that transition in the competition lift itself. Number four, one of my personal favorites, the pause deadlift. These are incredibly effective at teaching positional awareness and control, especially if you tend to rush your pull or if you have troubles with the start of the lift or start position. So, I typically recommend these are done two different ways. One for sumo, one for conventional. In the sumo deadlift, we want to pause within an inch of breaking the bar off the floor. Very, very bottom end of the range of motion. That's because generally in sumo, this is either where we lose position or it's the toughest part of the lift. For conventional, however, I generally recommend lifters pause a little higher. We want to feel like in this movement we're starting the lift twice. It's going to emphasize that bottom position. It's going to get you stronger off the floor. Another tip, pause it. Don't just start slow. Don't just like hiccup during the movement. Pause it. Hold it for a solid two count and then finish the movement. If you have to put a caption on it for somebody to recognize that you paused it, you didn't pause it. Lastly, don't take advantage of position during the pause. I see a lot of sumo lifters in particular lift the bar off the floor. Then during their pause, they'll wedge their hips in harder and get more upright. So coming out of the pause, they're in a totally different position and they're actually then advantaged out of that position. No, no. We want you to pause in the position you're going to be in. Come out of the position you're going to be in. We want this to be transferable to your competition deadlift. Exercise number five, the front squat. Yes, the front squat. Last but not least, the front squat. Now, a lot of people might think, "Hey, that's a squat. Isn't that better for the squat?" No, I don't think so. Especially if you're a even moderately trained powerlifter. Most trained powerlifters are not going to get enough leg push, you know, squat stimulus out of a front squat for it to be any good for the squat itself. So, I challenge you that this is in fact a better movement for the deadlift. That weight is in front of you. It's pulling you forward. You're working to stabilize yourself through your trunk and your core in an upright fashion. And you're using your legs, hinging, pushing while doing it. === FILE: Top 5 Squat Mistakes (That Are Killing Your Progress) [ZAopRzOV12E].en.txt ===

If your squat is stuck, feeling off, or is just uncomfortable, chances are you're making one of these five mistakes. I see these in intermediate, novice, all the way up to advanced lifters. And fixing these mistakes can help you on your path to building a big old squat. Mistake number one, incorrect bracing. The most common and fundamental issue that I see with lifters squats is their brace. Bracing is about more than just taking a big breath in before you squat. A lot of lifters mess this up by flaring the ribs way out and kicking their hips too far behind them, creating a whole bunch of extension on the descent of the squat. Now, this is an issue because you're going to have problems with getting to depth comfortably, or maybe you'll see a really pronounced sticking point as a result of it. In order to fix your bracing, what you want to be doing is contracting your abs super duper hard, clamping your ribs down on top of your abs, and trying to keep your hips tucked in, keeping your pelvis stacked with the rest of your back as you descend in the squat. Ideally, you want to maintain this position throughout the whole of the squat, which requires that you learn how to hinge and understand how to hinge. If you want more information on this bracing topic specifically, there's a couple videos we'll link in the description. Mistake number two, improper upper back positioning. A lot of lifters will struggle with creating a good shelf for the bar to rest on when squatting. And my tip here is that we need some degree of pulling the shoulder blades back and down to create that shelf. If you look at more novice lifters, a lot of them will be shrugged up in the shoulder blades and maybe even pushed forwards in the shoulder blades. This can result in them having issues with their wrists and elbows and shoulders in terms of discomfort and also in being bullied around by the bar. We need to be tight and rigid in the upper back in what I call the shelf in order to have a good squat. So, make sure that we're creating tension in the upper back and using that to tie the bar into our aforementioned brace. Mistake number three, driving your chest up. There used to for a long time, especially when I first got into powerlifting, be a very prevalent cue. Lifters should drive their chest up when squatting that once you hit the hole, just just push your chest up, reach your chest up. This is maybe one of the worst cues out there. Now, I don't think it's as prevalent anymore, and this kind of does double back on or piggyback on the bracing queue, but a lot of lifters will hit the bottom and then try to drive their chest up to ensure that they're not getting pulled forward by the bar. In actuality, like I said previously, this is going to mess with our brace. So, what we need to be doing in the squat is when we hit the bottom, we need to be keeping those ribs down and being patient out of the bottom. The first portion of the lift where we drive out of the hole, we should be focusing on maintaining the brace and pushing with the legs really hard. That way, we're setting ourselves up to be stronger and better positioned for the second and third thirds of the lift. Mistake number four, poor elbow positioning. I think a lot of lifters in the squat will try to use their elbows and either pushing their elbows forwards or backwards to try to make up for a lack of tension in the upper back. When lifters drive their elbows forwards out of the bottom of their squat, they're trying to make up for the fact that they haven't created a stable and tight upper back position to start with. And by wedging the shoulder joint underneath it as they come up, in some cases, you can have what approximates to a band-aid solution in keeping the upper back tight. However, in the long run and with maximal or super maximal weights in the case of a powerlifting meet, this will break down. The other issue with elbow positioning is a lot of more novice lifters who maybe aren't good at creating a stable shelf to unrackck and walk out with will push their elbows up behind them to to flare their shoulder blades off of their rib cage and create a shelf for the bar. This is because they're afraid to be in any kind of hinge when picking and unrackcking. My advice when it comes to elbow position, and this will kind of logically follow if we get the shoulder blades and upper back packed the way we need to, is that with your elbows, if you're going to think about queuing them, think about queuing them in towards your sides or in towards the center of your low back. Imagine there's a bullseye in the middle of your low back. You're trying to pull your elbows towards it. This should help you put your shoulder blades in a position where they're going to be tight and stable, and you're not going to need to be jerking your elbows forwards or backwards to make up for that lack of tightness. Mistake number five, incorrect foot pressure. Now, incorrect foot pressure is a bit vague in general, but that's because it covers a few different faults. So, let's talk about some of the more common issues. Probably the most common issue with incorrect foot pressure is when lifters rock too far forwards on their feet in the bottom of the squat. A lot of these lifters are very self-aware. They know they have a tendency of falling forwards. And part of the issue is that they're trying to fix that before they start the squat by being way far back on their heels. When these lifters are so far back on the heels, they are inevitably going to have to shift their center of mass forwards when they hit depth. This is going to cause them to pop much more far forwards than they'd like. And the fix for these lifters is to actually start with a little more pressure on the fronts of their feet. If you have this issue and you can start with a more balanced foot pressure, thinking about finding pressure both on the ball of your feet and the heels before you start and then just work to maintain that throughout the squat. Tempo squats can be kind of helpful there just so you can feel out each of the positions as you move through. Then you're going to be able to just stay balanced instead of trying to overcorrect and then falling forwards. Anyways, the next common issue with foot pressure is when lifters end up on the insides of their feet. Now, this one often coincides with sliding or popping forwards at the bottom, but it's also usually a symptom of being perhaps too wide in the stance and too towed outwards. If we have that issue of popping forwards and the stance is wide and the toes are out, then we end up not only popping forwards, but falling onto the insides of the feet. If you're a lifter who falls onto the insides of their feet in the bottom of the squat, my first place that I recommend you look at making changes is going to be in your stance width and your toe angle. Generally speaking, these lifters should narrow their stance up, even if just slightly, and bring their toe angle a little more towards straight forwards. This can help just allow the knees to track where they want to based on your hip strength and anatomy instead of forcing yourself into a position where you then have to change it to produce force on the way up. These squat mistakes can show up over time and they don't fix themselves. So, if you want some help with fixing these things, if you want coaching that's tailored to your specific mistakes in the squat and some good programming on a beautifully well-built app that has all kinds of cool metrics and a giant program library and all of the good things. and so bad. calgary barbell.com/training-app intros and outros. Like 70% of the video I will do in 5 minutes, but intros and outros I'll spend like 25 minutes on intro.

=== FILE: Train Your Brace： Accessory Work for a Stronger Squat #powerlifting [mCzdBMLti9Q].en.txt ===

Secondly, my tip for you is to train your brace. We talked earlier about the importance of learning how to brace, developing the skill of bracing, but if you're not already, I think at this point, you can start trying to intentionally affect your brace with the training that you're doing. Now, this can be from an SSB or paused squat or pin squat or something like that. Or in a lot of cases, what I recommend intermediate lifters do is to sort of break out the muscles that contribute to the brace and train them with isolation movements. Get on doing some rows. Get on doing some back extensions. Get on doing some side bends. Load that stuff up. Do rows both heavy and light in the six to eight rep range and the 12 to 15 rep range. Do some planks. Find a couple ab exercises that you suck at and get good at them. A lot of the times breaking out this work and isolating the muscles responsible for the brace can contribute and make sure that your brace comes up at the same level or same speed as the rest of your squat.

if you're struggling at all with your bench press technique let me give you a couple of tips that have really helped me work on not only being stronger out of the rack but on holding my shoulders in a better position throughout the whole bench press I've been coaching powerlifters and training my own bench press for many many years at this point and up until recently the biggest and most important cue I think somebody could have would be to pull their shoulder blades together as hard and as far as possible and pull the shoulder blades down as hard and as far as possible in the bench setup now I still think this can be a pretty useful queue for a lot of people especially more beginner lifters but I think there's actually a possibility that this queue like any or many others can be overdone to the point of being detrimental so here's my advice go ahead and get set up pretty much as usual lot of retraction lot of depression what I like to do is get the retraction first and then use my leg Drive scoop myself up the bench bit by bit until I have a whole bunch of depression and then here's the trick right here's the thing I want to change and here's what I changed for myself is before unracking instead of maintaining all this depression I get just the tiniest little bit of a shrug up you can hopefully see it there tiniest little bit of elevation tiniest little bit just so that when I go to unrack everything's locked in a bit better place and then I try to maintain that same upper back t tension throughout the rest of the lift and I find there's a lot less reorganizing I have to do when I get the bar out I think if you overdo the depression not only are you pretty much just doing a skull crusher out of the rack I think it goes hand and hand with being over tucked in the elbows but I think at this point you then have to reorient your elbows once you set your butt down you're probably going to have to move your shoulder blades around anyways so hopefully you could see what I was talking about there just that slight little bit of allowing some elevation just the tiniest little bit before the unrack for me that's allowed me a way cleaner unrack I've been able to self unrack where previously getting a handoff was such a huge change and such an improvement that there was almost no point for me to do a heavy single without a handoff this has allowed me to be a lot more self-sufficient and a lot better at the self handoff and it's also ensured that I'm not losing position off the chest as I initiate the press the other downside of being over depressed is that when you go to press a lot of times those shoulders are going to pop out of position anyways so I hope that illustration was sufficient let me know if you have success with this or if you're === FILE: WHAT IS RPE？ [0_JJZHKUV5U].en.txt ===

hey guys Bryce here again at Calgary barbell the strength Edge U I'm just going to talk a little bit about RP today so first and foremost what is RP stands for rating of perceived exertion uh it's a system that me and a lot of my lifters use predominantly uh as opposed to percentages sometimes in conjunction with percentages to monitor the intensity levels of our training so we use it as a reps left out of 10 uh is essentially how we we would monitor our RP so if you could have done two more reps on a set that's an rp8 if you could have done one more rep on a set that's an rp9 uh the system was popularized in powerlifting by a guy named Mike tashir uh who happens to also be my coach so I've learned a lot from him about how to implement the system and uh how to work with it I think it's important to establish a base idea at least of what an RP feels like as a beginner because it can help you start to get in tune with your body and how you'll react to training of varying intensities I also find it very effective to use to find a working Max on a given day and make sure that your training is where it should be why use RP uh there's a multitude of reasons I find it's very important for making sure that you're not over or undershooting your percentages to make sure that your percentages are lining up with exactly where you are that day uh it's again really effective to learn what heavy moderate and light loads and sets feel like uh and it can ensure that each each session of training is purposeful in okay this was supposed to be a moderate day this was supposed to be a heavy day sometimes the percentages don't necessarily line up with that because you come in feeling really good or really poorly and percentages don't necessarily adjust for those fluctuations in your performance from day to day so how to use RP uh one of the ways like I said that we predominantly use it is doing a single at an 8 RP to start your day off you can do this in the competition lifts or you can do this in a variation say a long pause bench or something like that either can be very useful to find a training Max for that day and then you'll base your percentages for your subsequent work off of that the other way we can use it is on sets of volume so you can do four reps at an eight or four reps at a nine and this is just a great way to adjust for like I said daily fluctuations in strength levels being a little stronger a little weaker a little overfed underfed didn't have a good sleep whatever we can accommodate for that with RP by monitoring how each set feels and how it moves personally I like to record most sets so I have a little bit of subjective and a little bit of objective in terms of finding that sort of midpoint to to find out exactly what my RP is going to be for that set you know sometimes it might feel like a nine but you watch the video and it looks like a seven so I would call that 78 so one thing about RP training is it can also be very complex it's got a bit of a steep learning curve it's kind of hard to explain so let's go through an example of how to use RP both to establish an estimated one rep max based off of work that you've already done or to predict a working set based off of an established Max so in the first case if I've already done the work set and I want to find my one rep max based off of that performance what I'm going to do is in this example uh I squatted 220 kilos for one rep at an eight so we're going to go through the chart and we're going to find out that one rep at an 8 is roughly 92% so what we're going to do is we're going to take 220 kilos we're going to divide it by .92 that's going to give us our estimated one rep max based off of that work set so we can use that Max to predict further workouts so let's say we have a Max and we're trying to predict what we should do for our single at an eight what we're going to do then is we're going to go through the chart again again we're going to find that one rep at 8 RP is 92% so we'll take our Max and we'll times it by 92 this is going to give us our estimated working set based off of our Max a really important part about doing RP effectively is ramp up sets so let's say you want to do a set of four at 220 kilos and you want that to be a nine what you're going to do before that is you're going to take 95% and 90% of your 220 kilos and you're going to perform two sets one at 90% of 220 one at 95% of 220 and the idea is that we're going to go 7 8 9 in terms of rpes the reason that's so important is because if you feel uh your your first ramp up is too light or too heavy then you can adjust on your way up to make sure you hit the RP you're going for a lot of times if you just jump into it and you do one working set then you're going to find you'll be over you'll be under you'll be a 9 and A2 or you'll be an eight whatever but if you do your ramp up sets properly and they feel like a 7 at 90% an 8 at 95% and a 9 at 100% of your goal weight that'll give you a good indication of your progression for the day same thing for an rp8 your 90% should feel like a six your 95% should feel like a seven and your n or sorry and your 100% of === FILE: Want a Bigger Bench？ Eat More #powerlifting [-B1DPH8QdtM].en.txt ===

The second thing, and this is slept on at all levels, is to eat your bench up. What I mean by that is focus in on your nutrition. One of the first things a lot of lifters notice if, for example, they cut down a weight class is that their bench is the first thing to be impacted. If you're not at the very least getting sufficient protein in in your day, you're really selling yourself short on bench progress. Even if you're not okay with gaining weight and and maybe your training is a vehicle for you to actually lose weight, ensuring that you have an adequate intake of protein throughout your day is by far one of the easiest boxes to check off to ensure that you're going to make some good bench progress. And conversely, if you're somebody who's looking to gain size and strength, eating in a surplus, it's going to be one of the surefire ways to increase your bench.

=== FILE: Want a Bigger Squat？ You Probably Need to Squat More [Rq0s8H-i0sE].en.txt ===

Number two, it works for bench. It works here too to some extent. You need to squat more to squat more. Strength training and the adaptations from resistance training in general exists in what's called a dose response relationship like a pharmaceutical like Tylenol or something. The more you get, the more effect. And just like a drug, too much can cause unwanted side effects. What I'm recommending here is if there's room, you can probably implement more squatting. If you're only squatting once a week or if you're only squatting a total of three sets a week, you can add more. And if you're a novice, you're probably going to be able to add weight almost every session.

The E1 RM goes up, presumably you're stronger. It can be hard to tell sometimes if you hit three reps at a six at a certain weight and then three reps at an eight with more weight.
