=== FILE: Weak Triceps？ This Bench Variation Fixes That [zLUyymCxgEw].en.txt ===

Next up, the close grip bench press. The close grip bench press is a great variation both because it is quite similar to your usual bench, but different enough. The benefit of this is that you'll have a separate training max. So the intensity will likely be a little bit lower and the pattern will be different enough that you can have maybe a little bit more bench exposure where you otherwise wouldn't be able to have comp bench or wide grip bench exposures. Ideally when we're using this as a variation we're going one to three fingers widths narrower. And in some cases, I will prescribe as a variation very close grip bench where we're coming into the edges of the knurling. But for example, I bench with my middle finger on the rings and when I do my close grip, I come into pinky finger on the rings. So it's not a massive difference, but it's enough that the movement feels different and is functionally trained a bit differently. The other main benefits of the close grip bench is that it's going to hit your triceps and your front delts maybe a little bit more than your normal bench pattern would. So, if we are actually a little weak at the top end or just a little weak in the triceps, adding in some close grip bench is a good way to kind of even out that strength curve so that we can get the bench progressing again. So, the main differences execution-wise with your normal grip and your closer grip bench are going to be that your normal grip, you're going to have a little bit of a higher touch point and your elbows are going to be flared out a little bit more. Right? Note the touch point. Note the elbow position. If I bring my grip in to where my close grip bench is, which is only about, like I said, two fingers width, you'll notice that the touch point is going to be further down my chest and my elbows are going to be more tucked. So, those things should happen relatively naturally. But if you're wondering why, like, okay, my close grip feels so awkward. Maybe you're not tucking enough. Maybe you're trying to mimic your usual bench a little too

=== FILE: What the F#$% is RPE？! [Part 1] [iTCoLIlvG8E].en.txt ===

since people started lifting weights there's been discussion and in many cases disagreement about what the best way to get big and jacked and strong is we've seen percentage-based training we've seen the bulgarian method and starting strength and the west side method just to name a few but there really is no one optimal way to train the smartest lifters and the best coaches are going to look at this smattering of approaches as tools in a toolbox and the more tools you have in your toolbox the better equipped you are to deal with nuanced and complex and individual situations today i want to talk about one of my favorite tools and maybe one of the most misunderstood tools from said toolbox and that is rpe first off what is rpe now rpe is used in strength training as an adaptation of something that used to be known as the borg scale now the borg scale went from 6 to 20 and was used in the context of cardiovascular research the reason the scale went from 6 to 20 was it correlated with heart rates between 60 and 200 to create an easy way to communicate how hard something was to researchers that could then try to draw some comparisons but because well 6 to 20 is a pretty tough scale to actually judge anything on from a subjective point of view it was changed to the modified dwarf scale which went from one to ten then along came mike to shear and he began to adapt to the rpe one to ten scale to specifically power lifting and more broadly strength and resistance training basically rpe attempts to define the performance of a set based on how many reps you had left in the tank when you were done if you do a set and it feels like you could have done two more reps after you rack the bar then that was an rpe8 if it feels like that was an absolute all-out max attempt grinder that was an rpe 10. we also use .5s in our rpe ratings sometimes for example if you're not sure if you could have done one or two more that would be an eight and a half now you can use rpe for any rep range although it becomes difficult past about 10 to 15 reps you can also use it for any exercise although it's definitely easier to use with larger more compound movements another note is that we don't really use anything below an rp5 it can be really tough to tell if you could have done seven or eight more on that last set so basically anything below an rpe5 we just call it warm up i think if you grabbed a really large set of the strongest lifters from the past 30 or 40 years most of them would tell you that they trained by feel at least to some extent the thing is training by feel and learning to sort of intuitively understand how much more or less to put on the bar how many more reps sets whatever to do it takes years of practice to understand how your body works in that way the whole idea of rpe is that it simplifies that process by creating a language that we can use to ascribe certain values to certain difficulties and creates a commonality wherein lifters can be taught how to do this and can learn how to do this at an accelerated rate because of a common language so by allowing people to discuss training whether it's athlete to athlete or coached athlete or athlete back to coach it essentially creates a scenario like going into the matrix and coming out knowing kung fu i know rpe show me even as a relatively new concept in strength training rpe has a fair bit of research to back its usage a 2018 study by some of the biggest brains in strength and conditioning research dr eric helms and dr mike zordos investigated the efficacy of using rpe as both a tool to estimate load and to make training judgments this study found that rp was not only a valid way to estimate resistance training but also a good way to gauge intensity near limit loads the same study also found that rpe based training may even provide a small 1rm advantage to a majority of trainees the long and short of it is that rpe is a commonly accepted and utilized tool for both researchers and the best strength and power lifting coaches out there and has been studied enough that we can reliably say it works at this point it is likely the best tool that we have at our disposal when it comes to auto regulation in training and now you might be asking yourself what the heck is auto regulation and why should i use it now auto regulation is basically just doing more or less based on how your session is going so you can do this by adding or removing load to the bar if you're performing really well and i would gather or or guess that a lot of people watching this video probably do this anyways if you're having a really good day you do a little bit more if you're having a really bad day you do a little bit less these are the same kind of feedback and response systems that coaches will use to adjust athlete training protocols on a longer scheme just within a session now you may be asking yourself is auto regulation good again we can refer back to the data one 2016 study found that a simple questionnaire better predicted and monitored athlete training response when compared to physiological and biochemical markers which obviously can be much more objectively observed another study this time from 2010 found that progressing load using autoregulation as opposed to a classic linear progression model resulted in bigger increases in 1rm bench 1rm squat as well as a 225 for reps test in div 1 football players in conclusion not only is auto regulation a useful tool when compared to other modalities but rpe is clearly a reliable method of applying autoregulation in a systematic fashion thank you for coming to my ted talk basically what we're driving at here is that in the long term the idea behind rpe and auto regulation is that you learn how to adapt your training on the go based on how it's going on a day that you go into the gym and you're performing well and the bar's moving fast and your technique feels good you should be allowed to take advantage of that and on days where it feels crappy and your technique feels off and the bar is moving poorly you can do a little bit less and overall that's probably going to have a net positive impact now the next big question is how do i incorporate rp into my training and honestly we could and we will make a whole other video on that and some of the intricacies of applying it to your training but what we're going to do for now is we're going to leave you with some basics on sort of how to get your feet wet with rp if you've never used it before the first thing you want to === FILE: When Squats Beat You Up, Use This #powerlifting #squats [hkytBrclfqo].en.txt ===

The fifth and final accessory movement that I want to include here is the leg press. Most gyms have one. While it might not be the most specific, and you might know a number of people who can leg press a lot and can't squat for it can be a really great tool if the bottleneck in your powerlifting training is getting more work on your legs. Because this doesn't load the back, you can get away with hammering volume on this thing. And I also just have a personal bias towards it. When I was rehabbing my knee and coming back from 2 years of my knee feeling like absolute garbage, this baby made it feel better every time. Things to note about the leg press are number one, get a very full range of motion. Doing quarter reps on the leg press is akin to curling in the squat rack, and you don't want to be that person. When you're using the leg press, I would try to do something similar to your squat stance on here if you can on the plate. And also the back angle on most leg presses is adjustable. So adjust it up or down so you can get a more comfortable experience. A lot of the times when I hop onto a leg press and somebody else has had it set, feels terrible. You adjust that back angle correctly, you're smooth sailing. There are great many other non-specific leg building exercises that you could include on this list. hack squats and belt squats and other kind of contraptions, pendulum squats and things like that. I'm sure those are all great. Go ahead and try those out if you want. But I like the leg press.

=== FILE: When to Add Weight to the Bar (Most Lifters Get This Wrong) [DS3VLxJbzSo].en.txt ===

It's the age-old question. How do you know when to put more weight on the bar? Do you just add 5 kilos to the bar every single time you see it and hope for the best? Whether you're an advanced or a beginner lifter, knowing when to push and knowing when not to push is the difference between progressing and spinning your wheels. The first thing we need to know about when we're talking about progress is progressive overload. that is the basis for all results we will get from training. What progressive overload means is we're adding volume or intensity or some amount of work over time. Today, I'm going to take you through how to know when to add weight, how to know when not to add weight, and how to reframe things or what to focus on if you're feeling stuck. If we're going to talk about progression, we need to talk about progression models really quick. There are plenty of them. I'm going to talk about three. There are more. I'm going to talk about three. And trust me, this baby can fit so many models of progression in it. Okay. So, the first of these progression models we're going to look at is what's called linear progression. Now, linear progression dictates that pretty much every time you do a session or week to week even, you're just going to add weight. And presumably that's going to work for quite a while when you're a beginner because not only are you going to adapt quickly cuz this these are stimuli that you maybe never experienced before, but also you're developing on multiple levels. you're going to be developing in terms of putting on muscle, putting on strength, and the coordination that's necessary to do movements like squatting, benching, and deadlifting. Those adaptations are going to happen fast. Therefore, you'll be able to just add weight pretty much every time you approach the bar. Number go up. That is the crux of a linear progression. If you're doing a 3x5 or a 5x5 and your plan is just add weight each time, that's your classic linear progression. You're going to make gains quite quickly, meaning you will have adapted and likely recovered by the time your next session rolls around. Hence, the ability to add weight after a period of time though, this stops working as well. The second model of progression we're going to look at here is a wave progression or undulating progression. After a while, linear progression is not going to work anymore. Once you're of runway on your linear progression, you want to start planning some fluctuation into your training. Usually, this looks like a period of time where you intentionally decrease volume while increasing intensity, hit a little reset, and then repeat that process again. If you look at most of the 50 plus expertly designed programs in the Calgary barbell app, that's their general structure. The basic idea behind this progression structure is that you build up, back off, and then repeat. By manipulating the variables of rep ranges, the intensity, maybe even the number of sets, you'll move from adding weight each week to now adding weight each block. So, you'll be able to prolong that progression as you get more experienced. The third progression model we're going to talk about here is autoregulated progression. Autoregulation is just a fancy way of saying that on days where it's there, we're going to go harder and on days where it's necessary, we're going to pull back and maybe go lighter. Imagine. By far the best tool when it comes to autoregulation is going to be RP or rate of perceived exertion. Now, I fully recommend that every lifter, regardless of whether you're using RP to regulate your training or not, learn how to use RP. It's an immensely useful, if not necessary, skill for spending a good amount of time getting good at lifting. And because it's a skill, you're going to need to practice it to be able to implement it correctly. An advanced lifter's training program is probably going to use any number of these different methods or or models of progression and is going to rely heavily on fatigue tracking and RP to autoregulate loads and bar speed in order to make sure that we're getting the appropriate stimulus at the appropriate time. In a lot of the programming that I write for the lifters that I coach, it may look more like a linear progression, but we're relying really heavily on reviewing each block afterwards to see what worked and didn't and hyperindividualize the programming as well as relying very heavily on RP to guide our load management. Okay, so at the highest level, you now have an idea of how to organize your training so that you can continue to make progress. But how about when it comes to each individual session or exercise? I'm going to give you some tips for how to know when you should add weight and then when you shouldn't. Okay, so the first indicator that you can probably go up is going to be bar speed. The bar is flying and you're moving smooth. Lifts are clean. It's a good sign. If your lift feels average, maybe repeat it the next week and try to get that bar speed up before adding weight. Indicator number two, if the RP is lower than what's programmed, if you're supposed to do a set at RP8, but you rate it a six, obviously you've got room to go up. Now, to give a little bit more specifics about that, if you're one or more RPS under what's prescribed, I'd say go ahead and go up in that session. But if you're only a half RP under, count it as an undershoot. You crushed it and add weight the next week. The third indicator I've got for you is minimal technique breakdown. Yes, we need to strain. We need to push against heavy weights. And sometimes reps get a little sloppy. I don't want anybody to be terrified of tiny little nuances and changes in technique because that [\h__\h] is normal and it is fine. But I like to apply the rule of 80% that I got from Mike Tash to Shear. You want 80% of your reps to look about 80% good as far as technique. 80% perfect or better. Do they have only one or two minor errors to their technique on a on a hard set? You don't panic over it. you don't reduce the weights or or anything like that. I've seen lifters who hold themselves back on progress because the technique is not absolutely perfect, but this is a long-term thing. Eventually, you get to where you can correct this. If you're checking those boxes, then you're in the clear. All right, so now let's talk about three examples of when you should not add weight to the bar. I call these the three nigh nighs. I have trouble saying no. I say nigh nigh. It's easier for me. Number one, if there's too much technique breakdown nigh nigh. Now, I mentioned the rule 80%. That still stands here. But if every single rep is reinforcing breakdowns in your technique that maybe you're trying to fix, well, you're not going to be able to fix those if you're just doing bad reps over and over again. Neigh neigh. There are some edge cases where you can progress in weight and get stronger while fixing technique issues, but you have to be executing your reps well in order to do that. Number two, if you're absolutely grinding out every rep. Yeah. Hey, [\h__\h] Yes, in order to get stronger, we need to strain against weight. I get it. But we also need to be able to accumulate a decent amount of volume. Training your competition lifts does not need to be a grind fest. And if you're hitting RP1 on the second rep of what should be a set of eight, give your head a shake. Neigh neigh. The last one is if your externals are poor, right? If you're not sleeping well, if you're not eating well, if you're overly stressed, if you're feeling super fatigued, those might not be good times to be expecting to take big jumps in weight and make a ton of progression. Yes, there are times where we'll be able to progress despite externals being bad, but you should adjust your expectations and be realistic going in if you know the odds are stacked against you. So, it turns out Kel Supre that there are other ways to progress beyond just adding weight to the bar. And the first of those ways is to add or remove sets or reps. Let's say you're running a 3x5, right? That's your progression. 3x5, you just smacking weight on there every week or every time you squat. Who knows? How can you progress that once you come up against it? Well, you could do a 3x six and and try to keep the weight the same. You could do a 3x4 in order to add more weight without failing or overshooting. Or you could do a 4x5. You could add or remove sets of reps to make it more reasonable to progress for longer. You can also try implementing accessory movements. If you're stalling out on the big three squat bench press deadlift, try out some variations of those movements. You can check out the video that we just did recently on my top five deadlift accessories. I think probably in the description below or maybe on the screen somewhere here. === FILE: Which Squat Accessory Do YOU Actually Need？ #powerlifting #squats [j5UeghPBPvM].en.txt ===

If your bench press is stuck or worse yet regressing, I'm willing to bench willing to bench willing to bet that your bench bar path has something to do with it. In today's video, we're going to break down what a bench press bar path should look like, why so many lifters get it wrong, and the one exercise that I recommend to fix it, the pin press. Cool. First, let's talk about the issue and why so many lifters mess up the bench bar path. Now the issue is that when lifters press the bar in the first few inches as the bar leaves the chest they will either a lose shoulder position and start pressing the bar out away from their shoulders or b they will allow their elbows to relax too much and come out behind the bar leading the bar to just kind of list out away from the shoulders on its own. === FILE: Why You Need to Think Less in the Gym - But More in Programming #powerlifting [T6C9_TpAEu8].en.txt ===

You know, like I said, however, as we become advanced, we love a contradiction. So, as we become more brain dead in our execution of the lifts, we have to at the same time become more cerebral with our prescription. What I'm talking about here is individualization. We need to have a system that we work within when it comes to prescribing weights, sets, reps, accessories, etc. You need a system for your programming and you need to be able to record, analyze, and iterate within said system. You need to be able to pick out what works and what doesn't for an individual lifter. And it's a tall task to work with an advanced lifter and still find progress. It would be really hard for me to break down real quick what is individualization, but that won't stop me from trying. So, here we go. Number one, understand your system. Whether you're using conjugate, bottom up, top down, periodization, whatever the hell it is, you better know that thing in and out so you know which knobs to twist and which buttons to push to make changes to it. Number two, record and analyze data. If you're not even writing things down, or better yet recording into some sort of spreadsheet or app like the Calgary barbell training app, you're doing yourself a disservice. The best coaches in the world have systems for analyzing the feedback from lifters. what works, what doesn't, are able to analyze sets of data and parameters over time, like E1RM in a certain rep range based on accessory movement selection, whatever that might be. And number three, don't change too much at once. This is a big part of the reason that I'm such a huge fan of bottom-up periodization and repeating micro cycles. Just Google those terms if you're interested. Keeping things consistent allows you to pull the signal from the noise. If everything is changing all the time, if you're cycling rep ranges every single week, if every exercise changes in every block, it can be really hard to tell what worked and what didn't or come up with any reasonable conclusion on why that might be the

=== FILE: Why You Should Be Using an SSB #powerlifting #squats [7yE_TWiNxT4].en.txt ===

This baby right here, this is called an SSB or a safety squat bar. It's one of many bars that you can use that have a little bit of camber on it. Right? You can see this little bend. When it's on your back, it's going to put the bar or sorry, put the weight slightly out in front of where the actual bar sits on your back. So, in some ways, it's going to mimic a front squat. It's going to be very challenging for your upper back and your trunk. Holding that bar and keeping it stable through the squat pattern is going to be one of the harder parts of this movement. But unlike the front squat, which if you remember I said was not a great squat accessory movement. And the reason that I think this is is because you can load this up and it's not going to fall off of you. You will be able to build this to the point where it is still challenging for your legs. And in specific, I think it's a really good tool for building a lot of quad strength, especially if you're a lifter who folds in the upper back and then has their hips shoot up behind you because the bar is going to pull you forwards more like a front squat or a high bar squat. My biggest tips for the SSB are going to be that you don't need to push or pull the handles. I get a lot of questions from lifters whether they should be pulling the handles into themselves or pushing up on them. Just don't worry about that so much. === FILE: Why the Pin Press FIXES Your Bench Bar Path #powerlifting [QHB5_38mxzQ].en.txt ===

Why the pin press? Why does this work so well? Why does this correct bar path? Well, it's because of the momentary relaxation of those supportive and postural muscles in the upper back. Because we relax even just slightly onto the pins and then need to retighten everything as we press. It teaches us to tighten everything as we press or to lose less tightness in the bottom. So, in that way, it can really carry over to help refine your touch weight and touch position in the comp bench. The other thing I really like about the pin press is the feedback that you get. So, if you go to press the bar in the wrong direction because of the relaxation, because of that momentary lapse of tightness on the pins, it's going to let you know that bar is going to go flying in the wrong direction. You're really going to feel the difference between a good bar path rep and a poorly pathed rep. So that feedback can go a long ways to exaggerating the fault and forcing you to almost overcorrect it that you can then take forward into your competition bench to help fix the bar path.

=== FILE: Your Elbows Are Sabotaging Your Squat [ZMQt_TxFl38].en.txt ===

Mistake number four, poor elbow positioning. I think a lot of lifters in the squat will try to use their elbows and either pushing their elbows forwards or backwards to try to make up for a lack of tension in the upper back. When lifters drive their elbows forwards out of the bottom of their squat, they're trying to make up for the fact that they haven't created a stable and tight upper back position to start with. And by wedging the shoulder joint underneath it as they come up, in some cases, you can have what approximates to a band-aid solution in keeping the upper back tight. However, in the long run and with maximal or super maximal weights in the case of a powerlifting meet, this will break down. The other issue with elbow positioning is a lot of more novice lifters who maybe aren't good at creating a stable shelf to unrackck and walk out with will push their elbows up behind them to to flare their shoulder blades off of their rib cage and create a shelf for the bar. This is because they're afraid to be in any kind of hinge when picking and unrackcking. My advice when it comes to elbow position, and this will kind of logically follow if we get the shoulder blades and upper back packed the way we need to, is that with your elbows, if you're going to think about queuing them, think about queuing them in towards your sides or in towards the center of your low back. Imagine there's a bullseye in the middle of your low back. You're trying to pull your elbows towards it. This should help you put your shoulder blades in a position where they're going to be tight and stable, and you're not going to need to be jerking your elbows forwards or backwards to make up for that lack of tightness.

=== FILE: You’re Pulling Too Early - Fix This for a Stronger Deadlift #powerlifting [DCyALkWB6Pw].en.txt ===

Okay, so let's dive in really quick to what I mean by pulling back too early or pulling too much and not pushing enough. When I talk about pulling too much or pulling too early, this is what I mean. When we break the bar off the floor, we go to pull back too early. We're trying to extend the hips and back before we extend the knees. What that's going to do is it's either going to have us push the bar forwards, pushing the bar further away from our center of gravity, or it's going to have us essentially working to try to pull the bar through our shins, which if it isn't blatantly obvious is inefficient. We're trying to bias and prioritize knee extension to start the lift and think about the initiation of the lift like a leg press. So, we're staying over the bar. We're pushing the floor away, right?
